title: Anna Howie
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Anna Howie

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Anna Howie 
 
 511
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Anna Howie, 49, is a resident of Easton and the current District 5 member of the Talbot County Board of Education. She was appointed to the post by Gov. Wes Moore in October, 2023.Howie is the assistant principal at Federalsburg Elementary School. She is married and has three children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the District 5 seat of the Talbot County Board of Education to represent students, families and other stakeholders. We are making gains in our school district, and I want to continue to ensure that our students and teachers have access to high quality instructional materials that will have an impact on student achievement and success.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities align with the goals set by the members of the Board of Education and the superintendent, Dr. (Shraron) Pepukayi. My two main areas of focus are increasing student achievement in the areas of mathematics and reading, and recruiting and retaining quality teachers.
Having teachers that provide outstanding instruction to our students will ensure that our students will be academically successful.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces, and how do you think the board needs to address it?
The most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools face right now is providing exceptional education opportunities for all students while being fiscally responsible.
Currently, the curriculum coordinating committee has brought high quality resources to the board for approval in the areas of reading and mathematics. These resources are paid for through educational grants. Utilizing grants is a responsible way of ensuring that we are providing our students with high quality instructional materials while being fiscally responsible.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
The postcards that have been mailed out focused on student test scores as well as other concerns. In terms of student test scores, we have purchased new high quality instructional materials. Our 2024 data reflects growth in all subgroups as well as certain subject areas and grades.
Student test scores are not just a concern for our district but across the State. Through the Governance and Accountability pillar of the Blueprint, expert review teams will be visiting schools across the state to review literacy and mathematics instruction in our classrooms and provide quality feedback for improvement.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
I believe that the pillars of the Blueprint reflect the areas that all Maryland Schools want to address. Those pillars address early childhood education, high quality and diverse teachers, college and career readiness, more resources for students to be successful, and governance and accountability.
The Blueprint identifies and prioritizes the needs that we see in our district and across the state. In order for our students to be college and career ready by 10th grade, we need to start addressing their needs in pre-Kindergarten and ensure that they are receiving the resources they need to be successful in every grade.

title: Ann O'Connor
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Ann O'Connor

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Ann Oconnor 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Ann O'Connor, 55, is a resident of Easton. She is running for the District 2 seat on the Talbot County Board of Education.She is a former teacher and has six children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the school board because I am deeply passionate about children's education. As a former teacher and mother of six, I have dedicated my career to helping children reach their highest potential.
Having witnessed my six children go through (Talbot County Public School), I have observed a decline in academic rigor, expectations and accountability, both in behavior and academics. This experience drives my desire to make meaningful changes on the school board. The fact that our students are scoring 18% proficient in math and 55% in reading indicates a pressing need for new perspectives on our educational strategies.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are the ABCs of education: advancing academics, boosting accountability and cultivating character. The focus is on the whole child. We cannot advance academics without discipline.
When students develop self-discipline, good character naturally emerges. This requires daily practice and consistent reinforcement of rules and clear expectations for all students across all buildings. Disruptive behavior must be addressed promptly and effectively.
Regarding academic accountability: A 95% graduation rate when less than ¼ of our students are proficient in math skills, and less than ½ are reading on grade level is inconsistent — something is broken here and we need to fix it.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces and how do you think the board needs to address it?
The most important issue is the steady decline of academic rigor. We need to make sure we continue to implement early intervention in elementary schools to support those who need that extra push. It's essential to send home books and ensure that our children have access to/and are accountable for reading materials throughout elementary, middle and high school.
We should place greater emphasis on traditional learning — using pencils and paper, cursive writing, fostering reading and critical thinking skills, while reducing reliance on computers. We need to offer pathways for middle school students interested in college or the workforce, including advanced/honors classes.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
The postcards received in the mail are snapshots of where our schools stand. No one wants these scores, they are abysmal. It's a wake up call to attack the problem and change the way we have been doing education here in Talbot County.
We need to put our focus on reading, writing and math. Our students are distracted. Let's eliminate anything that detracts from our mission as educators and focus on what truly matters — educating the child. Let's get back to basics with my ABCs of education.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
Simply changing a name doesn't lead to improvement. Over the last two decades, this initiative has gone through four name changes. Although there are many wonderful proposals in the Blueprint, I don't believe that top-down programs created by education experts would make our local schools better.
The Blueprint is a blanket principle mandated for all 24 counties in Maryland. The counties have no say in how it is implemented. It removes the schools from the control of locally elected school boards and puts control in the hands of unelected officials. I believe we want control over our local schools.

title: Public Safety Agencies Commended for Efforts in Car Crash
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Public safety agencies commended for efforts in car crash

 August 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 328
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - "There's not words to say thank you," Morgan Dailidenas said at the Aug. 15 Dorchester County Council meeting to a group of 24 local public safety providers.On June 22, Dailidenas' 4-year-old son Will was in a car accident around Route 50 and Maryland Avenue that caused a serious head injury. Because of inclement weather, aviation was out of service and Will had to be transported to Tidal Health in Salisbury via ambulance."Initially the child's outlook was unfavorable," Council President Lenny Pfeffer said at the Tuesday meeting. "However, after several surgeries, the child has been released from the hospital and is undertaking therapy." The Dorchester County Council commended the 24 service members for their efforts in the situation."Your steadfast dedication to preserve the life of another is an example of your commitment to serving the public with courage and compassion," Pfeffer said.He said that if it wasn't for the "rapid response, quick thinking and support" from Dorchester County Emergency Medical Services, Dorchester County 911, the Cambridge Police Department and the Rescue Fire Company, the results of the crash could have been much worse.Some members from the Rescue Fire Company were unable to make it to the meeting for the commendation, Pfeffer said.After the commendation was read, Will and his parents came up to thank the personnel from each agency."It was quite a morning, and the quick response is why he's here," Will's father Mike Dailidenas said. "I know they did the work at Tidal Health, but we needed to get there first. It all starts somewhere, and it started with you guys. Thank you."

title: 'Team effort' is what it takes to build and retain businesses in Kent
author: WILL BONTRAGER
content:
'Team effort' is what it takes to build and retain businesses in Kent

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 912
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — In a recent interview, Jamie Williams noted that in Kent County, businesses are coming and going regularly."It's a churning process," she acknowledged.
For instance, Rock City Cafe's last day was Oct 12. Then Oct. 15, at that same location, 21536 Rock Hall Ave., Little Lemon Leaf Diner is advertising a hiring event, for kitchen and dining room.
Some new businesses moved in recently as well. Starbucks is now open for business, and It's Masala Time, an Indian restaurant at 3 Washington Square, had its soft opening on Wednesday, Oct. 2.
As director of Kent County Department of Economic and Tourism Development for 11 years, Williams sees this turnaround daily, offering support and creating opportunities for businesses to thrive.
While working with the Economic Commission, business owners and leaders in the community appointed by the county commissioners provide guidance and insight.
Their goals line up with the county's comprehensive plan: to retain and expand businesses while supporting start-up businesses.
With a hefty schedule to close out the week, Williams, highlighted some projects her staff is working on.
Millington Senior Housing: The Millington Senior Village is a project that will provide 52 one-story apartments for people age 62 and up.
The project is located on land once part of the Millington Elementary School property.
The county is working with Millington during the grant search process. If successful, they hope to build a community resource center, food pantry, church and daycare center, centralizing services in one location.
With all that activity, Williams hopes to have Delmarva Community Transit services to accommodate residential needs.
"The more density we have the more services we can build there," Williams commented.
Railroad Upgrade: Williams pointed out the Worton railroad system, services five companies and was in a state of disrepair for quite a while. The county had received funding from the state to fix the tracks in May of 2020.
Williams was happy to announce that in September 2024 that project is finally completed.
The fact that from the time they had received the funding to the actual repair was four years, she said, should give an indication to the public of how slow-going these processes sometimes take.
Brownfield Properties: Williams and staff has identified 12 brownfield properties — places contaminated and needing remediation.
Most of these properties, the director said, were dry-cleaning establishments, dealing with chemicals. One of these is in Chestertown, Admiral Cleaners, located across from the 7-Eleven on 212 Maple Ave.; a building that sits dormant with graffiti on the walls.
Williams asked, is it worth the county adopting a brownfield credit, a state program. Is it worth going through that kind of process to redevelop the properties?
They are seeking answers to those pressing questions.
Recreational Cannabis: Beginning July 1, 2023, individuals in Maryland at least age 21 could legally use and possess the personal use amount of cannabis. Licensing is issued by the State for those who aim to start a dispensary.
Currently, Williams said the county issued only one micro-license, for a cannabis dispensary in Millington.
According to earlier reports, the establishment is under Rahul "Rocky" Dutta and if meeting all the requirements, will be located in the vacant Truist Bank building at 400 Cypress Street.
In talking with Dutta earlier in the week, Williams reported everything is moving forward.
Short-term rental tax:The county has been working with the municipalities to collect short-term rental tax from properties where AirBnb's or Vrbo properties or other rentals of that nature are located.
Williams acknowledged that is an extensive process involving lots of moving parts.
She had worked with her administrative specialist Rose Osborn to locate the properties throughout the county. They purchased software to track these properties more efficiently as well as send out notices.
Now it seems like they are seeing positive results.
According to the July report, Williams said "64 percent of properties are in compliance."
The director expects higher in the future.
"We feel we're going to see the biggest impact after the September numbers."
Other than using the tracking software, they worked closely with the municipalities to coordinate their memorandum of understandings for short-term rental tax, so they are all on the same page.
The county collects the taxes monthly and remit it to the towns. The towns receive 90 percent of the revenue with 10 percent going to the county for administrative costs.
Even before they purchased the software, Williams and Osborn have been working steadily on this issue since November 2022.
She was thankful for the cooperation that occurred since then.
"Getting all five towns together is an example of what we need to be doing for a lot of other projects," she said.
Business Retention and Expansion: Williams maintained they have always responded to the needs of business owners. However, now, that attention and focus is being formalized as they launch their Business and Retention Visit Program, starting last week.
The department has reached out to 10 or 11 businesses so far, refining their data-gathering process and consulting with business owners.
They've been all over the county, visiting KRM Development, Hickory Stick and Blue Heron Oyster House to name a few.
The qualitative information they gather will be assessed and used to help the community.
All of this would not be possible without Economic Development Manager Katie Abbott, the Kent County Chamber of Commerce and many others, Williams noted.
"It takes a collaborative effort from everyone; that's how economic development happens."
As a team, they are helping businesses find their niche area to succeed in a region specific to rural concerns.
"We're not an area to put up a big distribution center," Williams said."We're here to promote businesses focusing on what's unique and special in Kent County."

title: Caroline Commissioners Approve Summer School Grant
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commissioners approve summer school grant

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 17 | Section: News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - After expressing appreciation for the contributions of public health professionals, the Caroline County Commission held about an hour-long meeting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Nov. 21.Jamie Beachy, director of Caroline County Recreation and Parks, presented a grant award from the Maryland Department of Education to fund Caroline County summer learning centers.The commissioners accepted the three-year $1.2 million grant."What this means for the first summer year is that we will be looking at five school sites, and unlike our previous years that we targeted 700 students, we will be targeting 1,100 for next summer," Beachy said. "Yes, we are insane. We're fully aware that that's going to be a very big lift for us." Beachy said that for the two years following 2024, "without another funding stream becoming available, we will drop back down to three elementary schools with a total of 400 students." In other business, the commissioners approved a $1,011,834 contract with Nashville-based Wellpath LLC to provide medical services for inmates at the county jail.Two surplus vehicles will be offered for sale, deemed by the County Commissioners to be "no longer needed, outdated, unsafe, or (their) condition has deteriorated to the point that maintenance costs exceeds its practical value." A 2012 Dodge ambulance with 211,797 miles and a 2014 Dodge Ram with 218,742 miles will be auctioned locally.Ryan White has left his position as director of the Department of Public Works, and that position may be reconfigured before it is advertised.Commission Vice President Larry Porter expressed some concern about "the scope of what is going to be able to be done by public works." "At some point, in my opinion, (it's) going to have to be reduced. There's going to have to be more things contracted out," Porter said.Commission President Travis Breeding said, "I've been giving this position a lot of thought, and I think it would be helpful to have someone there who is wellversed in the design process, permitting process, bid process.I almost feel like it's a two-person role." The next Caroline County Commission meeting will be held 9 a.m. Tuesday, Dec.5, in Room 106, Caroline County Courthouse, 109 Market St., Denton.Meetings are held 9 a.m.Tuesdays except the fifth Tuesday of the month, unless announced otherwise. Meetings are open to the public for attendance. Attendees will be security screened as they enter the courthouse.All Commission agendas with hyperlinks to documents can be found at www.carolinemd.org.The public can also attend meetings and work sessions remotely via ZOOM at https://zoom. us/j/300062187. The tollfree phone numbers to dial in are 888-475-4499 or 877-853-5257, and the meeting ID number is 300 062 187.

The Caroline County Commissioners recognize National Apprenticeship Week Nov. 13 to 19 in Caroline County. The week celebrates the power of apprenticeships as a vital workforce training model, empowering individuals to gain valuable skills and secure higher incomes. The commissioners offered thanks to Bilbrough's Electric, Bob Breeding General Contractors, Choptank Electric and Lywood Electric for their commitment to sponsoring active registered apprenticeship programs and shaping the workforce of tomorrow in the Caroline community.

title: Lack of funding a 'recipe of frustration'
author: STAFF REPORTS
content:
Lack of funding a 'recipe of frustration'

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORTS | Section: News 
 
 1210
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Upwards of 200 individuals gathered at the Queen Anne's County Public Schools Board of Education building in solidarity of Queen Anne's County Education Association members raising their voices against proposed employee layoffs as the board held a closed executive session Aug. 20."We teach our students to collaborate and talk together, well, let's walk the walk," Education Association President Cecilia Mitchell said about the assembly.
Marching from Centreville Elementary School to the building at 202 Chesterfield Avenue, teachers, parents, students, supporters and members of the education union wore "red for ed" against cuts proposed in an effort to balance the district's budget.
According to the meeting's agenda on the board website, the closed session was held "To consult with counsel to obtain legal advice; To conduct collective bargaining negotiations or consider matters that relate to the negotiations."
Creating "joyful noise," as Mitchell put it, the rally attendees carried signs of support for school staff and verbally chanted against cuts. In front of the building, participants inscribed chalk messages on the sidewalk.
"People love the school systems here. The future lives in that building," Mitchell said, pointing to nearby Centreville Elementary.
"It's deeply frustrating that QACPS wants to cut some of our lowest-paid educators who work directly with our students, and at the start of the year, no less. We don't know how many people, or what job titles," Mitchell said in a statement ahead of Tuesday's rally. "There are any number of ways to deal with budget problems, but not if you won't talk to your educators."
According to a press release issued by the Association, they were notified on Aug. 14 of the potential layoffs of "an unknown number of QACPS support staff, who are among the lowest-paid employees in QACPS."
The Association seeks the superintendent and school board to address the budget shortfall before pushing it on to employees, Mitchell said.
The layoffs announcement came after the school district asked Queen Anne's County educators on Aug. 12 to accept five unpaid furlough days during the 2024-25 school year.
The educators association said they asked for documentation to justify the furloughs and were "sent no response nor documentation, and then refused to meet on any of the dates offered to discuss the matter."
Seeking budget transparency, the Association has filed a formal information request, with questions including where the money was going, and what is being done that doesn't involve cutting positions, according to Mitchell.
"So, we just have two questions for Dr. Saelens. First, why are you asking us to cut our salaries if you won't ask the county for additional funding, and second, why won't QACPS answer our questions about the budget crisis like the law requires?" Mitchell said.
Other measures needed to be exhausted first before the proposed Reduction In Force and layoffs of essential support staff, she said.
Mitchell highlighted the effect layoffs would have on the livelihood of support staff, who ensure the optimal running of the school, while making up the smallest portion of school system employees, "And they make the least amount of money," she said.
According to a statement from Superintendent Patricia Saelens, the school system sought to balance the budget through attrition.
Saelens noted the "severely underfunded Blueprint For Maryland' Schools, coupled with overall inflation has created a recipe of frustration" — a deficit that Queen Anne's County is not alone in facing, she said.
As a result of that lack of attrition there is still a current shortfall of two million dollars. Saelens wrote in a letter to staff on Aug. 19, "This summer, we have worked to do a detailed budget analysis and determine what could be cut to put those funds into salaries. We have identified numerous items to help reduce the budget shortfall. We will cut scanning, tutoring and locally funded conferences. We will reduce our legal line item. We will cut school block grants by 10%."
Additionally Saelens wrote the district is canceling the Cenergistic Energy contract, and repurposing the staff tuition reimbursement line. "While these measures will help, it is simply not enough to balance the budget," she stated, "Under Maryland Law, a local board of education is prohibited from carrying a budget deficit."
Saelens contends the district met with the union on July 18 and 31 to discuss a retirement incentive and potential furlough days. The retirement incentive was not successful as only two employees took advantage, still leaving them under the attrition necessary to balance the budget.
Together with the union, Saelens said they selected dates that purposely would not impact student days. "We also determined the proposed furlough days would be for all employee units, including the superintendent and all administrative staff. These proposed five days would have avoided the need to reduce any member of our staff," she said, "We know that each of our employees are vital to the successes of students. It was our intention to keep our staff whole."
Saelens said they provided the union with all the information they requested within 24 hours, meeting again on Aug. 6 and sharing a draft MOU regarding proposed furlough days.
Given the upcoming start of the school year, we requested that they provide us with their decision by Aug. 12, Saelens said. The union responded in writing informing leadership that they "formally decline Queen Anne's County Public Schools proposal of furlough days for the 2024-2025 school year".
As a result, Reduction In Force (RIF) letters were issued on Aug. 14, in accordance with the RIF process outlined in the negotiated agreement, Saelens concluded.
Whether proposed furlough dates or RIF, the teacher's union has a ratified contract based on an offer the BOE presented to the union that was accepted, according to Mitchell.
"We must take care of each other," she said.
Showing support for fellow union members and district bus drivers, Tony Mansfield stated the rally was a "good start" and sought collaborative efforts to come up with a budget that does not include reductions and a solution that honors the contract ratified in June.
School psychologist Julie Rock, of Matapeake Middle School and Kent Island Elementary School, stated it was her job to advocate for students and the rally highlighted the invaluableness of the various support needed within the walls of the schools. "Right now, the students that need us the most are going to be losing the support," Rock said.
Standing alongside QACEA was Lori Hrinko, President of Cecil County Classroom Teachers Association. "This isn't about you wanting more, this is about what's right for our kids," Hrinko told the crowd.
Hrinko encouraged everyone to be involved in their school districts, as students represented the future generations.
QACEA is a local affiliate of the Maryland State Education Association (MSEA), which in turn is an affiliate of the National State Education Association, and Mitchell voiced appreciation of the organizations' support.
Working to promote change through action, Mitchell hoped to inspire students of all ages and showcase that change is possible.
Mitchell noted issues cannot be addressed by avoiding dialog or shifting blame, "Problems can only be solved with conversation, creative solutions and direct contact," she said.
Moving forward, Mitchell seeks to have all groups unite with the same underlying goal: identify the best interests for the good of students. "[Working] together; real numbers, real decisions," Mitchell said.
More information about QACEA can be found at https://qacea.org.
The Board of Education will next meet for a regular meeting Sept. 4 at 6 p.m.

title: Candidates Have Varying Views
author: Staff Writer
content:
Candidates have varying views

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 364
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The 2024 election season will see voters from several towns in Talbot County choose their representatives for the Talbot County School Board.There are six candidates and, while neither political party is formally endorsing them, they do have varying views concerning the education of our children.
Three are conservative and three are progressive. The conservative candidates are: Ann O'Connor (District 2), Karla Wieland-Cherry (District 5), and Kerry Gunshenan (District 6). The progressive candidates are: Cynthia Jurrius ( District 6), Anna Howie (District 5) and Candace Henry (District 2).
As a public service, the local chapter of a parent support group called Moms for Liberty hosted a debate for the school board candidates on Sept. 23 at the Easton firehouse. All six candidates were invited; four appeared, including Cynthia Jurrius and the three conservatives Ann O'Connor, Karla Wieland-Cherry and Kerry Gunshenan. The event was a success and helpful for parents and grandparents in deciding for whom they will vote to sit on the local school board. Another school board candidates' debate was held on Wednesday, Oct. 2, at 6 p.m. at the Avalon Theater and all six candidates were invited to speak.
While Moms for Liberty, according to several public statements made by the chapter Chair Jan Greenhawk, does not endorse any of the candidates, the Moms have been accused in a local periodical of "inserting their partisan candidates into a non-partisan position." Such an accusation is surprising in light of the fact that another school board candidates' debate was held at the Academy Art Museum, sponsored by the Talbot County Democratic Forum.
Sadly, only three of the candidates were invited to speak. And guess which three. Yes, the three more progressive candidates, who happen to be Democrats. The other three candidates, the three conservative candidates, were not invited at all. And yet Moms for Liberty, which has not endorsed a single candidate, is accused of partisanship? Why are liberals so afraid to hear the opinions of conservatives, especially as regards our children's education? Is it that conservatives put children's well-being ahead of the latest fads of social-engineering and psychological manipulation? Is it because conservatives want to truly educate the children rather than indoctrinating them with left-wing philosophies?
MARY-EILEEN RUSSELL
Claiborne

title: Karla Wieland-Cherry
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Karla Wieland-Cherry

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Karla Wieland-Cherry, 55, is a resident of Trappe and is running for the District 5 seat on the Board of Education.She is a registered nurse and an associate real estate broker. She volunteers with many local organizations. Wieland-Cherry said she grew up in a home that kept up with and often interacted with politics, both local and national. She is married and has two children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the Talbot County Board of Education to work to improve our local school system for students, parents and our community.
Goals I hope to achieve will be to improve test scores by enticing more qualified teachers to teach in Talbot County and retaining current teachers; raising education benchmark standards; increase use of CTE programs; improve student discipline rules; improve school safety measures; improve open communication transparency between schools, teachers, administration and parents and the community.
What are your priorities if elected?
After speaking with teachers in different grades at local schools, the constant concern I hear is the lack of student discipline and their safety as teachers. Teachers can't teach and students can't learn… and test scores can't improve… and teachers won't want to come teach in a county… if they are in an environment where everyone feels unsafe.
Teachers have a distrust of the current board and feel that they don't listen to them and take their concerns seriously. I want to rebuild that trust by listening to teacher concerns and addressing those in a more supportive manner to make necessary changes.
What is the the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces and how do you think the board needs to address it?
Lack of teachers and staff seems to be the biggest issue. As I mentioned already in the prior questions, my priority will be to listen to teachers and rebuild the trust that is currently missing with the present board.
I will also work to improve communication between schools, teachers, parents and the community and work to create a more secure learning environment for everyone.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
Everyone should take their own initiative to investigate local school data from reliable resources. These postcards are one way of bringing awareness to the community and open communication channels amongst parents, teachers, administration and the board to ask questions about their authenticity.
In speaking with many parents of all grade levels of students, I consistently hear that there is no open communication, especially with the current board.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
Teachers I've spoken with are frustrated and don't know Blueprint well, and what they do know is vague with no clear guidelines to how it's implemented. Funding Blueprint is based on inequities of and poverty levels of students for priority funding. Blueprint prioritizes equity learning.
We need to recognize every student's individuality and work to strengthen those individual skills for college/career readiness. We need to stop looking at certain groups as "minorities" and overlooking their skills as worthy individuals capable of learning instead of trying to make everyone "equal" to someone else.

title: Cynthia Marrah Jurrius
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Cynthia Marrah Jurris, 65, lives in Easton. She practices mediation law and is a director of conflict resolution programs. She is married and has three sons, all of whom graduated from Talbot County Public Schools.She is running for the District 6 seat on the Board of Education.
Why are you running for office?
Our public schools play a pivotal role in shaping our community's future, and we need board members who can help move (Talbot County Public Schools) forward to excellence. With a background in mediation and youth, school, family and community conflict resolution, I listen to all perspectives and value the richness in diversity of opinion.
I am a collaborative problem solver, skilled at helping people work together to solve complex community challenges. I want to ensure that our board continues to function effectively, advancing schools where every student can thrive. We have many strengths on which to build; together, we can solve any challenge.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are interrelated: fostering academic excellence, supporting educators and creating a thriving school environment. I am committed to advancing student mastery of essential skills, improving academic proficiency and preparing students for college and careers.
Ensuring we recruit, retain and support outstanding teachers is key to this vision. Equally important is providing a positive, safe, effective and inclusive school climate where all learners can succeed and promoting strong family and student engagement to build a collaborative, supportive community around our schools. Together, these priorities create the foundation for a bright future for our students.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces and how do you think the board needs to address it?
Advancing academic proficiency is a priority. Supporting a positive, safe, effective and inclusive learning environment is fundamental for student success, as well as teacher retention. Finding innovative ways to engage families, including non-English speakers, and students will support all aspects of student success.
The current board and superintendent are making progress toward addressing these issues despite many challenges, such as the COVID-19 learning gap. Through additional instructional support, expanding use of innovative community partnerships, strategic use of technology, targeted allocation of resources and engaging all sectors of our community, we can accelerate progress in these areas.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
I would like to see the sender of the mailers come forward for productive and honest dialogue. While improving academic proficiency is essential, the harmful attacks on our teachers, fueled by misleading and inflammatory rhetoric, seem aimed at undermining our public schools and inciting fear.
I would welcome an open, honest conversation about what this group seeks to accomplish, with accurate, relevant information. Let's work together to lift our Talbot County Public Schools to be the vibrant foundation of our community, where education is valued, everyone can belong and our teachers receive the support they need and deserve.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint for Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
The creation of the Blueprint was the result of a comprehensive effort with input from many stakeholders. The five pillars are: Early Childhood Education; High Quality and Diverse Teachers and Leaders; College and Career Readiness; More Resources for Student Success; and Governance and Accountability.
The TCPS team has a detailed plan for managing the Blueprint and provides regular reports on progress for public view. There are many areas of the Blueprint that are positive, however, the most challenging aspects are mandates without sufficient funding. I support continued efforts to address the funding formula as it has been applied to Talbot County.

title: Experience, Transparency Needed
author: Staff Writer
content:
Experience, transparency needed

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 387
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With so much attention on the presidential election, it's easy to forget the importance of local, down-ballot races. But decisions with direct impacts on our lives are made at the town and county level, and these elections deserve our thoughtful consideration. The upcoming Talbot County school board election is a prime example.I live in District 2, whose northern edge extends to Port Street, includes the southern part of Easton's historic district, neighborhoods around Idlewild Park and Easton High, much of the east side of Route 50, including Mulberry Station and south to Dutchman's Lane. The choice for us is between Candace Henry and Ann O'Connor.
Initially undecided, I tuned into the candidate forum. It was clear that both candidates are well-liked in the community, but it was also clear that Ms. Henry is vastly more knowledgeable about the state of our schools and the actions the school board is taking to improve them. Quite simply, she is the more qualified candidate.
For example, when Ms. O'Connor suggested asking departing teachers their reason for leaving, Ms. Henry pointed out that exit interviews are conducted and used to improve teacher retention. This pattern repeated itself several times, with Ms. Henry having specific answers where Ms. O'Connor did not. Ms. Henry also shared that teachers are already involved in curriculum development, something Ms. O'Connor suggested as a new idea.
But the flyers have made the decision crystal clear. You know what I'm talking about. Our mailboxes have been inundated with them. All contain cherry-picked data about test scores and spending with zero context. Lately these flyers have taken a turn toward incredible as they discuss "required reading" in third grade. Incredible meaning not credible.
The information in these mailers is designed to shock the recipient and the secretive nature of their funding raises red flags. A brief online search about the sponsor "Pay Attention America" leads only to a short-term office space in Wilmington, Delaware. Then last week a Republican friend showed me a flyer she had just received, authorized and paid for by the 1776 Project, a radical far-right group. They were endorsing Ms. O'Connor by name (as well as Karla Wieland-Cherry and Kerry Gunshenan, candidates for school board in Districts 5 and 6, respectively).
I'm voting for Candace Henry. We need experience and transparency on the school board, not hidden agendas.
ALISON SANFORD
Easton

author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado valvarado@chespub.com
content:
Newcomers win Talbot County Board of Education seats

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado valvarado@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 455

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Public Schools is looking at new leadership, according to uncertified vote totals from the Maryland Board of Elections.Cynthia Marrah Jurrius, Karla Wieland-Cherry and Ann O'Connor, none of whom have prior experience on the Talbot County Board of Education, won seats for their districts.
The elected board members said they plan to bring their campaign priorities to the forefront of their terms, which begin Dec. 1 and will last for four years.
Talbot County's Board of Education is made up of seven members from different districts in the county and two student board members. Districts 2, 5 and 6 were on the ballot in the November election.
For district 2, O'Connor won with 52.7% of the vote, according to the State Board of Elections, beating out incumbent Board Member Candace Henry. O'Connor said her campaign provided the opportunity for her to get a better understanding of leading a campaign, school board responsibilities and Blueprint, Maryland's 10-year plan to improve the state's education system.
O'Connor said she has just skimmed the surface and is ready to learn more.
She said she will be prioritizing academics and discipline. With academics, she said she would like to see elementary students reading every night and working on more book reports, and for schools to provide summer reading lists.
For discipline, O'Connor said she has noticed a lack of consistency, or "different rules for different people."
"We need a plan for all the schools that this is the way we're going to, you know, this is the dress, this is the behavior when you walk in the building. If you veer from that, there's going to be this consequence, and you got to, I mean, it's the follow through," she said.
For District 5, Karla Wieland-Cherry won with 54.6% votes, according to the State Board of Elections. Wieland-Cherry, who defeated incumbent Board Member Anna Howie, said she appreciated the support she received from her campaign, though she did mention she "got a lot of negativity." She hopes she can work through any negative sentiments to have a productive four years on the board.
Wieland-Cherry said she will be prioritizing open communication for everyone she works with and promoting the Career and Technology Education Program, which offers job training in various fields.
She said it's important to encourage kids to look at career alternatives for those not interested in college, whether that be training to become a firefighter, plumber or welder.
"I think (the CTE program is) under encouraged, under utilized," Wieland-Cherry said. "And that's where jobs are."
For District 6, Jurrius won with 51.9% of the vote, defeating Kerry Gunshenan, according to the State Board of Elections. Current District 6 Board Member Mary Wheeler did not seek reelection.
Jurrius did not answer calls from reporters in time for publication.

 CAMBRIDGE — December's Dorchester County Board of Education meeting was particularly important for each one of the board's five members.During the meeting Dec. 12, three members were sworn in for their term.
Also during the meeting, Board President Sheri Hubbard and Vice President Talibah Chikwendu, who are in the midst of their terms, were reelected by the board as president and vice president. They will remain in those roles for a year.
In July, Hubbard and Chikwendu were elected to their respective roles after former Board President Mike Diaz and former Vice President Susan Morgan resigned for separate reasons.
During the meeting Dec. 12, Hubbard thanked the board for their "vote of confidence."
"I will try to do my very best to serve you well," she said.
At the end of the meeting, other board members congratulated the two.
"Thank you for your leadership and for agreeing to continue," board member Chris Wheedleton said.
Wheedleton and fellow board members Brandy Dawson Cumberland and Christine LaMonica were all sworn in for another term at the beginning of the same meeting.
This will be Wheedleton, Cumberland and LaMonica's first full term. All three were appointed to replace former board members.
Wheedleton was appointed to the board in 2023 to replace former board member Laura Layton, who resigned from the board that April. Wheedleton won against Jerome Harris to maintain his seat in the recent Nov. 5 general election.
In July, both LaMonica and Cumberland were appointed to the board. LaMonica was appointed to fill Morgan's seat after she resigned in mid-June following a contentious board vote to terminate an alternative education contract.
Cumberland was appointed to fill Diaz's seat after he resigned in late June, citing family and health concerns.
Before being appointed, LaMonica and Cumberland had been running against Morgan and Diaz, respectively, in the 2024 general election. Both LaMonica and Cumberland ultimately ran unopposed in the November election, allowing them to stay in the roles they were appointed to for another four years.

title: Talbot Board of Ed Adds Makeup Day for Snow; Approves 2025-26 Calendar
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Board of Ed adds makeup day for snow; approves 2025-26 calendar

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Wednesday's meeting, the Talbot County Board of Education added a day onto the end of this year's school calendar following last week's snowstorm.Talbot County Public Schools was closed Monday through Friday last week due to snow that blanketed the Mid-Shore. However, the 2024-2025 school calendar only had four inclement weather days built in, meaning an additional day was needed to comply with the state's 180-day requirement.
Helga Einhorn, assistant superintendent of school leadership and student success, recommended that a day be added in June, moving the last day of school for students to Friday, June 13.
The last day for teachers would be Monday, June 16. Einhorn said that historically, most teachers complete mandated training that affords them with not having to come in on the last day.
The board unanimously passed the adjusted calendar for this year.
2025-26 CALENDAROn Wednesday, the board also chose the district's calendar for the 2025-2026 school year.
At last month's meeting, Einhorn presented a draft calendar with two days off in March and a five-day spring break, which was the recommendation of the calendar committee. Board President Emily Jackson, however, expressed frustration there weren't multiple options posed.
This month, Einhorn returned with three draft calendars. The first was similar to what the board saw in December, with a four-day weekend in March and the shorter spring break. The second draft removed the off days in March and had an eight-day spring break.
A third draft included both the March break and an eight-day spring break, pushing the last student day back to June 10, 2026.
All three drafts included the typical days off in November for Easton's Waterfowl Festival, as well as a winter break from Dec. 20, 2025, to Jan. 4, 2026.
"There is no calendar that we're going to create that is best for every single person," Jackson said.
Jackson said it's clear — based on previous polling and community input — that most families favor the extended spring break. Board Vice President Amy Dodson suggested the board move forward with the second or third calendars.
Board member Karla Wieland-Cherry said she preferred the first calendar with the shorter spring break.
"You're losing a lot of school time for eight days off for students," Wieland-Cherry said. "You're losing a lot of momentum. And plus you're concerned with providing day care. Not all employers are going to allow that. That's quite a long time to take off of work and find day care and so forth."
She added that not all families are looking for a longer spring break.
"My only concern is that if 59% of our students are at the poverty level, we're really talking about more of a smaller group who are really going to financially be able to afford an Easter holiday," Wieland-Cherry said. "… You really could possibly potentially be causing more hardship for something that's more an elitist type thing, quite honestly."
Jackson said while she agrees with Wieland-Cherry's point, she has "to go with what the community is saying."
"We have asked again and again, and the majority of the respondents to any time we've asked this have said they like that spring break," Jackson said.
Following board discussion, Jackson motioned for approval of the third calendar featuring two off days in March and five days for spring break. Her motion included an amendment to the calendar that the March days off serve as two of four inclement weather days for the district.
By a 6-1 vote, with only Wieland-Cherry voting against, the board approved the 2025-2026 school year calendar.

title: Dorchester County Public Schools Faces Budget Deficit
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools faces budget deficit

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 636
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County Public Schools prepares to submit its fiscal year 2026 budget to the county, it is also preparing for some tough conversations.With $86 million in expected revenues and $97.5 million in estimated expenses for fiscal year 2026, the district is facing a deficit. Currently, with carryover in funds from previous years, the estimated deficit is at $10.19 million.
"We've just got some difficult decisions to make as a district on how we're going to move forward with the current budget crisis that we're in," DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said during a Dorchester County Board of Education budget work session Thursday.
Jodi Colman, district assistant superintendent of academics and student services, said the budget increases for fiscal year 2026 make it possible to keep the district's current staff in place.
"This would just be to basically maintain the programs that we have right now," she said about the draft budget. "All of those increases were due to just keeping our staff that we have for the most part."
Thompson said "a whole host of things" has caused the deficit, mentioning fixed costs and unfunded mandates from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state.
Board of Education Member Brandy Dawson Cumberland said that although the board likes a lot of what the Blueprint aims to do, there are "certain unfunded mandates that are going to cut other things."
Thompson said the district is still waiting on exact numbers from the state and county. He said once they have those numbers, it is possible the deficit could be lower than $10.19 million.
"But I don't think that it will be higher than that," he said.
So far, the district has taken a number of actions to reduce the deficit, Thompson said. This includes:
Reducing some positions added with Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief fundingSending emails about non-essential spendingDeciding not to hire for vacated positionsReducing the central office custodian scheduleReducing student support monitorsMerging some job dutiesEliminating the education specialist position
"We did try to make some significant changes," Thompson said. "And there's more that I didn't put up that we have done. But the reality is it's not enough."
The district is looking into more actions that can be taken to reduce the deficit. Some possible actions include revisiting who should have board vehicles, auditing and reducing the number of programs and platforms the district uses, revising overtime policies, sharing resources with the county and reducing staff.
"No one wants this one," Thompson said about reducing staff.
While listing different "cost containment options" Thompson and board members made it clear that the district hasn't made any decisions yet, and is just looking at potential cost-cutting options.
"We are just at the beginning of starting to think about what things we can do to attack that number," Board of Education Vice President Talibah Chikwendu said.
"And that's why we really would like to have public input to know what the public feels are areas we should focus on if possible," Board President Sheri Hubbard said. "Because we want to do what's best for kids, bottom line."
The Dorchester County Board of Education will host another budget work session on Feb. 13. It will also hold one in March. The district's proposed budget must be submitted to the county in June.
Board Member Chris Wheedleton said that if community members are able to do anything, they should talk with their representatives in Annapolis.
"Because we need their help," he said.
Thompson urged that this is the time to work together and not be divided.
"Because at the end of the day, we know that $10 million deficit that we're in, that's going to hurt the kids," he said. "That's going to have a profound impact on how we can provide resources for our students."

title: Master Plan, Grant Application Approved for St. Michaels Park
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Master plan, grant application approved for St. Michaels park

 January 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Environment 
 
 676
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Months of work came to a happy conclusion Wednesday evening with the Commissioners of St. Michaels' unanimous approval of a final master plan for San Domingo Creek Park and a $1.7 million open space grant application.The final master plan for the park, previously referred to as the Boundary Lane Waterfront Park, includes nature trails, expanded wetlands, a living shoreline, a fishing pier, a comfort station and associated parking.
A long-wanted dog park was initially included in draft park plans, but following extensive debate, it was ultimately removed to extend the area of the park's pollinator meadow, said Scott Scarfone, an associate principal at Mahan Rykiel Associates who worked on the park design.
Leashed dogs will still be allowed to walk through the new park.
Plans for a defined dog park are still in the works, according to Town Manager Rob Straebel. A 2.4-acre parcel next to Bradley Park was identified as a likely location, and the town is working on a purchase or lease agreement for the site.
A viewing mound, a 10-foot hill with an accessible path to give visitors an elevated view of the creek, was also eliminated from the new park's final master plan.
The viewing mound will be replaced by a circular loblolly pine grove, with views of the creek still visible. The expansive pollinator meadow will extend into the center of that space.
Scarfone called the town's decision to buy the property and develop it into a park "wise" and "visionary."
"I can tell you that generations of people who visit this park are going to enjoy it in the future, so congratulations to the town for acquiring an amazing piece of property," he said. "I think it was a very smart decision."
The town purchased the 7.6-acre property on Boundary Lane, which is adjacent to San Domingo Creek, for $2.9 million last year. Formerly owned by nonprofit Environmental Concern, the property also includes an administrative building, which is slated for use as the town's new office.
Because most of the park is intended as open space, opportunities to receive state grant funding through Program Open Space are available to help offset the purchase price.
Nearly six acres of the property were designated by Talbot County as potential open space.
Appraisals of the open space acreage came in at $1.6 million and $1.8 million, according to Town Planner Steve Ball, leading to town staff seeking approval to apply for a $1.7 million grant for reimbursement of acquisition costs.
The request was approved unanimously. The grant application, due in the next few weeks, was set to be submitted Thursday.
Though master plan approval and the submittal of the grant application mark important steps forward in bringing San Domingo Creek Park to reality, more regulatory work remains to be done.
While the town owns the property, and over half of it is located within town limits, nearly three acres remain under the county's zoning jurisdiction.
The town is seeking to annex the remainder of the property into its limits, including Boundary Lane itself, which includes the property in front of the park's entrance. St. Michaels Police Chief Jeff Oswald also requested to include the road in the annexation, Ball said.
Neighboring resident Langley Shook and Commissioner Tad DuPont raised concerns about bringing Boundary Lane into the annexation.
"I'm leery about taking on the expense of maintaining a road when we are really pinched on every single front," DuPont said.
If the annexation is approved, the new portion will also need a town zoning designation.
St. Michaels doesn't have designated zoning for parks, and the part of the park property already within the town limits is zoned residential, Ball said.
The remaining area would need to be zoned as residential, and that's in part due to many state grants requiring the property to be in a priority funding area, an urban area where the state will invest money for infrastructure, Ball said.
The annexation request will be heard by the St. Michaels Planning Commission next month.
The town's board of zoning appeals will also consider a special exception to use the existing offices on the property as town administrative offices in February.

title: Community Invited to 9/11 Day of Remembrance Ceremony
content:
Community invited to 9/11 Day of Remembrance Ceremony

 August 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Economic Development Corporation along with community partners the Town of Easton, Talbot County Government, Talbot County Department of Emergency Services and the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce Young Professionals invite the public to a Day of Remembrance Ceremony on Sept. 11, 2023.Throughout the summer, volunteers have been working together to help strengthen relationships between members of the community by supporting projects that exemplified the theme, "We Are One: Community Supporting Community." The project is one of many across the country that will pay tribute to the individuals lost and injured on September 11, 2001, as well as honor the first responders and the many others who have risen to service in a crisis. The purpose of this awareness effort is to empower the general public to be caring, responsive community members should their fellow citizens need their support and to be mindful of the work of first responders in their community.The Day of Remembrance ceremony concludes the summer events."Easton is a resilient community, one that has supported its citizens through hundreds of years, through the good and the challenging times," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook. "I am proud of the summer-long project that helped our neighbors get to know each other and reinforce the idea that everyone will reach out and lend a hand across the city in times of need." Projects throughout the year included citizen responder trainings, a community mosaic project, community conversations and creation of downtown banners illustrating the theme."We are so grateful to be in such a supportive community.Teaching our community how to keep themselves and their neighbors safe is the first step in making our community resilient and able to endure whatever may come our way," said Geneva Schaffle, Talbot Emergency Management coordinator.This year's ceremony will incorporate volunteers from several local towns in the area, including the Easton Middle School Band and representatives from the Talbot County School system, local law enforcement officers and fire department volunteers, and members of local churches.Keynote speaker and Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher will remark on the significance of the ceremony to the Easton community. Following the ceremony, the public is invited to a reception at the Talbot County Free Library, which will feature works of art created by program participants."We Are One: Caring for our Community" is funded through The Arc of The United States through a sub-grant from Ameri-Corps, a federal agency that engages millions of Americans in service and leads the nation's volunteer efforts for Patriot Day and the national 9-11 Day of Service and Remembrance Project.The ceremony will take place beginning at 8:30 a.m. at the Service Memorial on the corner of West and Dover streets in Easton. In the event of inclement weather, the ceremony will be moved to the Talbot County Free Library on Dover Street.More information about the event is available online at discovereaston.com/weareone.

The purpose of this hearing is to solicit public comment on various proposed amendments to Chapter 28 of the Town Code (Zoning). Specifically, twelve amendments addressing a variety of issues are proposed The purpose of the proposed amendments is to correct oversights/omissions resulting from the original enactment of the comprehensive update of the Zoning Code completed in November of 2021, based upon the Planning Commission and staff's experiences in working with this new document.The public is hereby invited to comment on the proposed amendments.Such comments may be either submitted in writing at any time prior to the Hearing, or made in person at the Hearing. The complete packet of specific amendments is on file in the office of the Town Planner and is available for public inspection during normal business hours and may also be found on the Town of Easton's website (www.Eastonmd.gov). In general terms, the proposed amendments address the following issues:· The addition of Short-Term Housing as a Use in Table 312 A, the MXW USe Table.· Revisions to Table 2.1, the overall Table of Permissible Uses, with a focus on Uses 103.1 - 103.9, the "Middle Housing" use types.· The deletion of the supplemental standard which requires a 1,000 foot separation of liquor stores (and other uses, by reference) from certain other uses.· Revision to the examples of non-material changes to Planned Unit Development (PUD) projects.· Revision of the wording of existing language regarding architectural styles associated with multi-family apartment complexes, and clarification that certain of the supplemental standards for this use are not applicable to projects in the Central Business Zoning District.· The addition of a new supplemental standard applicable to all middle housing types intended to insure that any such use remains of an appropriate height in the context of the neighborhood in which it is proposed.· Clarification that graphics included in the definitions of Middle Housing types are for illustrative purposes only.· The addition of the use "Any Middle Housing Type or Variation not listed above", and associated supplemental standards, to enable consideration of a middle housing type not contemplated or described by the existing list of such uses.· Revision to the language describing how expired or soon-expiring PUD projects may be treated.· The correction of an inadvertent redundancy of the use "Live-Work Unit" in the Zoning Code.· Revisions to the language prohibiting the enactment of negative use restrictions concerning grocery stores by exempting grocery stores of less than 15,000 square feet from any such use restrictions.In addition, the Town Council solicits the public's input on two potential revisions to the draft amendments that the Planning Commission has forwarded. These are:· Continuing to maintain the more intense Middle Housing types as Special Exception uses in some zoning districts. This would mean Cottage Courts, Townhouses, Mansion Apartments, and Courtyard Buildings would remain SE in the R-10A and R-7A zoning districts, but would be outright permitted in the CB District. Fourplex stacked and triplex stacked would become outright permitted uses in all zoning districts.· Revising the language concerning the expiration of PUD approvals to allow for an initial approval of three years or a longer period if specifically requested and approved by the Town Council pursuant to their legislative approval (rather than the current two years).Persons wishing to attend or participate in the public hearing who require special accommodations or assistance because of a disability should contact the Town Clerk, Kathy Ruf at the Town Office, telephone number (410) 822-2525 during normal business hours by October 30, 2023.Kathy M. title: Pending Legislation Could Decimate Newspapers
author: Rebecca Snyder — Executive Director, Maryland Delaware DC Press Association
content:
Pending legislation could decimate newspapers

 April 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: REBECCA SNYDER Maryland Delaware DC Press Association | Section: Columns 
 
 726
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The members of the Maryland Delaware DC Press Association (MDDC) are deeply concerned about the potential consequences of HB1258 on local journalism. This bill, which is on the governor's desk now, would upend the longstanding practice of publishing public notices in local newspapers and their associated websites, threatening the vitality of Maryland's communities and the essential role of the press in fostering civic engagement and accountability.We believe that HB 1258 will create a seismic change in the local media landscape that will decimate and potentially prompt the closure of local news outlets.
For decades, local news media has been at the core of their communities, providing critical information, facilitating public discourse, and holding power to account. Although digital formats now supplement print publications, the watchdog role of news media has remained constant. Public notices, a cornerstone of transparency and accountability in government through independent publication and a deep reach into local communities, have been a fundamental part of this ecosystem.
However, HB1258 seeks to centralize estate notices on a government-operated website alone, effectively pulling critical information for creditors and heirs into a subject specific website that requires a user to have reliable internet access and to know where to look for the information. It also will remove a vital revenue stream for local newspapers, jeopardizing the future of journalism in our state.
The ramifications of this legislation extend far beyond the newsroom. By undermining the financial viability of local newspapers, HB1258 threatens the livelihoods of countless journalists, editors, and other media professionals who work tirelessly to keep our communities informed. Moreover, it potentially deprives readers of access to vital information about government proceedings and community events, thereby undermining civic engagement and transparency.
Cataclysmic change sounds dramatic. Local news, however, is on the precipice.
HB 1258 will abandon a system of public notice that has worked well for decades and eliminate a significant number of jobs in Maryland. Local news will go away if communities, governments and others do not support it. Studies show that when a community loses its source of local news, it experiences decreased voter turnout and civic engagement; increased municipal borrowing costs that lead to higher taxes; and decreased transparency among government and business officials, leading to increased waste, fraud, and abuse.
Proponents of HB1258 argue that centralizing public notices on a government website will increase accessibility and efficiency for the state Register of Wills offices. However, this overlooks the reality that many residents, particularly in underserved communities, lack reliable internet access or the technological literacy to navigate online platforms effectively. Many pandemic-era subsidies that made broadband access affordable for Marylanders have been discontinued. Websites are hacked regularly and government is not immune. The print publication is a tangible, permanent record that is archived by publications and libraries, containing the records of an entire community.
Having these notices appear only on a court website diminishes the independence of notice as the agency placing the notice is the one that is publishing the notice. News media is in the business of audience development and dissemination of information, and the traffic to both member websites and the MDDCNews.com aggregated site dwarfs a state website. Having notices in the context of other news and information the public searches for make notices more visible. That will not happen under this bill.
HB1258 was drafted without input from the very stakeholders it stands to impact most profoundly: local newspapers and the communities they serve. The absence of robust debate and meaningful consultation during the legislative process is a disservice to the principles of democracy and good governance. At its core, HB1258 represents a shortsighted approach to policymaking that prioritizes convenience over the public interest. By hastily dismantling a system that has served our communities well for decades, this bill threatens to irreparably harm the fabric of local journalism and the democratic values it upholds.
Our member publications are committed to their communities, employing local journalists and other professionals, occupying office space, contributing to the community and often serving as media sponsors and supporters of community events. All this will be drastically affected if HB 1258 becomes law. Those jobs won't come back; some publications will not be able to stay in business. Sustaining a $1.7 million hit industrywide will surely mean smaller newsrooms and shoestring operations.
Governor Moore, please stand for local news and veto HB 1258.
Rebecca Snyder is the Executive Director of the MDDC Press Association.

title: Baltimore Police Clear Homeless Encampment
author: Connor Bolinder; connor.bolinder@chespub.com
content:
Baltimore police clear homeless encampment

 August 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connor Bolinder; connor.bolinder@chespub.com | Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On July 21, Baltimore City police, first responders and outreach workers went in full force to clear out the homeless encampment at the corner of Dundalk and Holabird Avenues.A "No Trespassing" notice was posted earlier this month, stating that the area would be cleared on July 21.The Baltimore City Mayor's Office of Homeless Services and nonprofit groups visited the site before it was cleared to connect people with resources like shelter and drug treatment. The area was cleared by noon."Members of the Baltimore County Homeless Services Division have been working closely with Baltimore City officials to address the encampment near Dundalk and Holabird Avenues," Baltimore City police said in a statement sent to the Old Dundalk Neighborhood Association. "We understand how concerning it is to see this situation in your community. As the encampment is located on city property, the Baltimore City Mayor's Office of Homeless Services is leading response efforts in coordination with other City agencies, including the Baltimore City Police Department, Baltimore City Department of Public Works, and Baltimore City Department of Transportation with support from nonprofit organizations under contract with Baltimore County to provide outreach and access to services." People began living in tents on a strip of grass in front of the Holabird Business Park earlier this year.Community groups wrote to county and city leaders for months asking for a solution, but the encampment was located just inside the city line. The Baltimore County government doesn't have any jurisdiction on that property, but county police officers are often on standby just up the street.The Old Dundalk Neighborhood Association joined with other community groups on the city-county line: Boston Courts, Norwood-Holabird and Graceland Park. In February, they wrote a letter to officials to request a solution.People living in tents longterm poses a lot of public health concerns, and city police were regularly called out to the encampment.Several people in the camp used drugs during the daytime, and panhandling at the intersection was very common.Baltimore police Precinct 12 Capt. Glenn Wiedeck and City Police Maj.Kiera Saunders had coordinated for crime calls associated with the camp. It was a welcome collaboration between the city and county law enforcement."They're actually speaking to each other right now and that didn't happen in the past," ODNA President Jess Lilli said in April.Last month, the Baltimore County Continuum of Care Homeless Roundtable hosted a job and resource fair at the Sollers Point Multipurpose Center. The Baltimore County Homeless Services Division continually works to help people who are homeless and seeking help.Baltimore County Police issued a statement promising to help connect homeless people with resources, and prevent a similar encampment from forming in Dundalk."Though this is a Baltimore City operation the Baltimore County Police Department is aware of the impact it may have on the surrounding county communities and is taking steps to offer any homeless person(s) services and resources if they attempt to migrate into Baltimore County," BCPD said."Officers will also be in place to remind any of these homeless person(s) that the camp sites they are used to in Baltimore City will not be allowed in Baltimore County."

A Baltimore City garbage truck pulls up to the homeless encampment. Workers form the Department of Public Works hauled tents, leftover belongings and trash out of the area after police cleared it out..

Notice was posted weeks ago, alerting anyone living in the encampment that it would be cleared by city police on July 21..

author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels reorganizes police, OKs raises

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 282
 Words

 ST. MICHAELS - The Commissioners of St. Michaels voted unanimously Wednesday to revise job descriptions in the town's police department and approve raises in light of the new organizational structure.The need to restructure the small police department came about earlier this summer after former Chief Anthony Smith retired on June 30. Newly appointed Chief Jeffrey Oswald was sworn in the same day, leaving his former position as the department's captain unfilled.Instead of attempting to locate a new officer to serve as captain, with a salary ranging from $85,000 to $100,000, Oswald suggested restructuring the department through restructuring and promoting two of his officers to sergeants.The department's old structure included a chief, a captain and two corporals, each with two officers under them. The newly proposed and now-approved structure includes the chief and two sergeants, each with two officers under them.A memo in the town's meeting agenda packet indicated that both sergeants will be able to fulfill each other's roles, but each will have a separate primary focus in assisting the chief: one to help handle patrol responsibilities and one to aid in administrative tasks.Oswald said he previously handled the responsibilities of the captain position for 12 years while ranked as a sergeant and lieutenant and wanted to provide his officers with the same opportunities for advancement.The new structure will have a minimal budgetary impact, as the total base salary impact for the restructuring is $7,200.The promoted sergeants will receive mandatory first line administrator training and will be recognized by the Police Training Commission to take command in Oswald's absence. The positions come with a two year probationary period.

title: Suspect still at large following police pursuit
content:
Suspect still at large following police pursuit

 Page: B5 | Section: News
