 DENTON - A suspect was still at large Tuesday morning, Aug. 29, following a pursuit involving Delaware and Maryland police that began Friday, Aug. 25, near Marydel, Maryland.On Friday, officers from the Caroline County Sheriff's Office chased a wanted suspect through the northern part of the county before he escaped into a wooded area.The office's Criminal Investigation Division and several units were searching for Todd Randall Hockensmith, 36, of Felton Tuesday morning, according to Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker.According to a release from the sheriff's office, Caroline County sheriff's deputies, the Maryland State Police and the Delaware State Police went to a property Friday in Marydel, Maryland, looking for Hockensmith.At the property, Hockensmith was seen running to a car, which he used to flee the scene.Police pursued the vehicle through the northern portion of Caroline County until the suspect drove the car off the roadway in the 16000 block of Lentz Road in Henderson, Maryland.According to the police report, Hockensmith fled on foot and ran into a heavily wooded area. As other units arrived, a perimeter was set up and K-9 units were called to assist along with aviation units.After about three hours of law enforcement officers' searching the area, Hockensmith was unable to be located.Investigators learned the vehicle Hockensmith was operating had been reported stolen, according to the police report."The vehicle was reported stolen to the Denton Police Department by Hertrich Chevrolet (in Denton), and we actually located another vehicle on the property that was stolen from them that they didn't even know about," Baker said.On Monday, Aug. 21, Delaware State Police posted on its Facebook page a request for help from the public in locating Hockensmith, who "has three active felony warrants for his arrest for a host of offenses, including theft, burglary and a police pursuit." The Caroline County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigation Division responded back to the Marydel property where the incident began. A second vehicle was located and recovered that also had been reported stolen through the Denton Police Department.As a result of the on-scene investigation, deputies arrested a female associate of Hockensmith identified as Danyeal L. Shahan. Shahan is being charged with motor vehicle theft and related charges. Shahan was wanted through the state of Delaware. She is being held on bond at the Caroline County Detention Center, according to Baker.The Caroline County Sheriff's Office has active warrants for Hockensmith "for the two motor vehicle deaths (of) two brand new cars from Hertrich Chevrolet here in Denton," Baker said.This is an active investigation and anyone with information is asked to contact the Caroline County Sheriff's Office at 410-479-2515.

title: '25 Kids Should Not Take This Whole City Down' - Cambridge Council Grapples with Youth Crime in City
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'25 kids should not take this whole city down' - Cambridge council grapples with youth crime in city

 September 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Youth issues were the overwhelming theme for the third Cambridge City Council meeting in a row.At the Sept. 12 meeting, residents and commissioners alike made comments about juvenile crime.Lance Cephas, who is the father of Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioner Sputty Cephas, said crime is affecting everyone, including the children and families who aren't part of the problem.He further noted the children who aren't contributing to juvenile crime are being punished for the actions of about 25 children, "25 kids should not take this whole city down," he said.Lance Cephas stressed the importance of educating the kids that are caught doing things they shouldn't be."Because if you send them back home to that same environment, ain't nothing going to happen," he said. "A lot of police officers, they'll pick them up, they'll let them go, and soon as they're around the corner, they've done something else to somebody else. So you've got to get them and educate them." He said he understood both his children's, Lajan and Sputty, and Mayor Stephen Rideout's points of view regarding the juvenile curfew but said the council shouldn't be "at each other's throats" and "controlled by 25 kids." "We've all got to come together," he said.In late August, Rideout vetoed a juvenile curfew ordinance which commissioners had passed Aug. 14.Before that, in July, Rideout had proposed an alternative curfew ordinance which had additions and changes from the original curfew ordinance. These included adding definitions and altering language on enforcement procedures and penalties.Since Rideout vetoed the original curfew ordinance, Sputty Cephas has made amendments to Rideout's alternative ordinance in an effort to compromise and "find middle ground." According to council meeting documents, Cephas plans to recommend these amendments Sept. 25 when Rideout's proposed ordinance will be read for a second time.During the meeting, Sputty Cephas talked about finding that middle ground."Commissioner Atkiss made a point to say that $100 is a lot of money for a struggling parent," he said."My day job is in banking, so I understand that struggle as well." Sputty Cephas said he would like to keep fines as part of the penalty for not following the curfew, but said he cut them in half in his amendment. Instead of a $100 fine, it would be $50.At the end of the meeting, Rideout suggested to Sputty Cephas that the two of them get together to talk about the proposed amendments to the alternative ordinance. Sputty Cephas agreed to meet.Two presentations were given during Monday's meeting, as well. One presentation was given by Pam Gregory, president and CEO of United Way of the Lower Eastern Shore, and one by Lisa Molock, chief executive director at Let's Thrive Baltimore and an organizer for Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America.Molock talked about the work she has been doing in Baltimore, and Gregory talked about the economic issues that many Marylanders face. She shared data from a report that focused on asset limited, income constrained and employed (or ALICE) Marylanders and shared data on Dorchester County residents specifically. Gregory said that in Dorchester County, 45% of residents are below the ALICE threshold.During public comment, Theresa Stafford said poverty is a "lead driver" for many other issues in Cambridge."We need to get serious about fixing the problem of poverty," Stafford said."Bringing in industries or businesses that will pay good wages, and of course, supporting getting kids educated because that's the other key driver that keeps driving up the crime."

title: Ophelia a Bust but Still Causes Flooding
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Ophelia a bust but still causes flooding

 September 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 480
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HOOPERS ISLAND - Tropical Storm Ophelia caused flooding in parts of Dorchester County this past weekend."Luckily we didn't make out too badly with the storm," Dorchester County Emergency Management Planner Jimmy Windsor said.According to the National Hurricane Center, the storm made landfall near Emerald Isle in North Carolina Saturday.On Sunday, the center warned of continued coastal flooding "along portions of the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal rivers" for the rest of the day.Cambridge received 2.61 inches of rain between Friday, Sept. 22, and Sunday, Sept.24, according to the National Weather Service.The storm resulted in "moderate to borderline-major tidal flooding" in the county, particularly in its southern and far western areas, Windsor said. He added the areas most affected were the Hoopers Island area, Taylor's Island and the Wingate, Toddville and Bishops Head areas.Dorchester County Council member Rob Kramer monitored how the storm affected the county over the weekend.He said the road past the Hoopers Island Causeway "took a little bit of a beating." While the causeway had been closed Saturday, it has since been reopened.Windsor said Water Street in Cambridge also shut down temporarily due to the storm.Over the weekend, the Sheriff's Office was trying to limit traffic through Worlds End Turn as well, he said.The county's Department of Emergency Services had few, if any, flood-related calls over the weekend, Windsor said."I know the [Hoopers Island Volunteer Fire Company] assisted some people with getting back to their residences from places they were at on the island after it had started to flood," he said.As part of the county's contingency plan, the National Guard was brought into the county. Kramer said the county received the guards once Gov.Wes Moore declared a state of emergency in response to Tropical Storm Ophelia on Friday."They had brought a couple Humvees with them," Kramer said. "They were just a contingent plan in case we needed them." Windsor said while the county didn't end up needing assistance from the National Guard, it did some pre-deployment area reconnaissance "just to make sure they knew where they were going if they had to go anywhere." As of Wednesday, Windsor said most of the flood water has receded."There is still some high water areas in the lower part of the county, which is not being helped by the fact that we currently have a higher than usual tide cycle," he said. "But everything is back open." Windsor asked that the public use caution when traveling in those lower parts of the county in case the water has made it difficult to navigate the roads."In the grand scheme of things, this was minor compared to some of the storms we've had in the past," Kramer said.

title: Few Show for Police Town Hall Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Few show for police town hall meeting

 October 5, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 870
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Few residents showed up to a town hall meeting, hosted by the Cambridge Police Department Tuesday evening, to hear about the department's community policing efforts and its goals for the future.Toward the end of the meeting, which was held at the Empowerment Center in Cambridge, Police Chief Justin Todd asked the five residents in attendance to share information from the meeting with other residents."All I ask of you, is that you take this tonight and make sure that the information - whether it's good information or bad, if you agree or disagree - and you put it out there to the public that we, the police department, want to work with our community to better the situation out on the street," Todd said.While the department used to only have two or three officers in a community policing division, Capt.Shane Hinson explained that every officer in the department is now a community-oriented police officer."It's all of our jobs to go out and make meaningful connections with the community," Hinson said, adding that every officer has been through a training course on community-oriented policing.Todd said community-oriented policing is what the department "is and will be built off of." Along with Todd and Hinson, Capt. Antoine Patton and Lt. Greg McCray spoke at the town hall.Patton spoke about some of the things the department does to increase positive interactions with the community."If you look on the news, it would have you to believe sometimes that police officers are only there when bad things happen," he said. "But we want our community to know that we love them, and we're here to work together." Patton mentioned how the department takes children and senior citizens Christmas shopping every year. This year, he said he had the idea for "12 Days of Christmas" where the department will take children and senior citizens out shopping from Dec. 12 through Dec. 24.Patton talked about a Thanksgiving dinner the department hosted last year and plans to host again this year."In five to 10 years these children will be teenagers and these teenagers will remember the things that we did," he said.Todd shared some of the city's crime data at the meeting as well.Since 2019, the Cambridge Police Department has taken 114 illegal guns off the streets, he said.Compared the the record number of seven homicides in Cambridge last year, Todd said there have been two homicides so far in 2023."I don't call that success by any means," he said. "The day we have zero is the day we've been successful. [[---]] But it's progress. And that's what we have to keep banking on as we keep getting better as a community and a city." Todd said the number of juvenile crimes (committed by those under 18) is "continuously getting worse." "Out of the 300-and-some assaults that we've had this year, 127 have been committed by juveniles," he said.Todd brought up the juvenile justice reform bill, passed in 2022, which stops youth, under the age of 13, from facing criminal charges like assault and weapons violations.He said something needs to be done to fix this reform."And the juveniles know it," he said. "We have 12-year-old kids telling us, 'What are you going to do to me?'" With the juvenile curfew in Cambridge, which went into effect Oct. 1, Todd said the last thing he wants to do is fine a parent."But at the end of the day, if we can help one child or one family, one parent to better parent their child, and get them out of the streets, then we've done something right as a community and it's a start," he said about the curfew.In 2010, Todd said the department had 52 officers. When he entered the role of police chief, there were 29 total officers with two in the police academy."At that time, we had a department that was depleted," he said.The department is building itself back up. Todd said there are 39 total officers in the department right now, with four in the police academy."So we'll get those out of the police academy in December, and we'll keep building our Criminal Investigations Division," he said.Todd said he hopes to increase the diversity of the department. He said that 67.5% of both civilian employees and sworn officers in the department are white. Black employees make up 22.5%. Hispanic employees and Asian employees each make up 5%."We want to mirror our community," Todd said, acknowledging that this is no easy feat."But I just want the public to know we're working hard to get there," he added.After the meeting, Gary Gordy, one of the residents in attendance, said that he thinks more policing is needed in Cambridge and thinks it's good the department is hiring more officers. He said that when it comes to crime, Cambridge needs cameras.Gordy added that some of the problems the city is facing with crime could have been prevented if the city had acted earlier."We wait for years to get things done," he said.

title: Serving, Protecting for 250 Years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office Celebrates Its Sesquicentennial
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 979
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - To mark the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, a new badge has been struck, containing symbols of its history dating to colonial Maryland.But the badge itself is a symbol of the long line of sheriffs who have held the office since 1773, when Thomas Hughlett of Greensboro was appointed by the British governor after the county was formed from parts of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.Bookending the long blue line is Sheriff Donnie Baker, who, like Hughlett, is also a Greensboro native. He's the county's 77th sheriff.Caroline County Deputy Lt. Jacob Andrew is the unofficial historian of the sheriff's office. And because he's the fifth generation of the Andrew family to serve the office during the past century, he's well-qualified for the job."Jake was just teaching me something," Baker said. "I didn't know that the first sheriff was buried up there (in Greensboro)." According to Andrew's research, Hughlett was a plantation owner appointed to a one-year term by the governor to be in charge of weights and scales because he was deemed trustworthy.Ironically, the next year he became captain of the Caroline County Militia Fifth Company, which encompassed Greensboro, Goldsboro and Bridgetown during the American Revolution.Hughlett later became a judge. He is buried in a crypt in a tiny, privately-owned graveyard in a Greensboro subdivision, the site of the Hughlett family farm.During the Civil War, John Wilson Saulsbury served a two-year term from 1861 to 1863 and was required to swear allegiance to the Union.Andrew said Sheriff James Temple, who served from 1923 to 1926 "was actually a pretty cool guy." A veteran of the Spanish-American War, Temple was known as the walking sheriff."He had the first Buick in Caroline County. He always told everybody that," Andrew said. However, "he hated driving it.So, if he had to go serve a warrant on somebody, he'd walk from Denton to Ridgely, lock them up and walk them back." "The original sheriff's office was pretty much a shed on the courthouse green, and it was very easy to break out of," Andrew said. The lynching on the green of Federalsburg blacksmith Marshall Price following accusations of murder in 1895 prompted the government to build a new jail across Gay Street on the Choptank River, where it stands today.In 1921, William Curtis Andrew, Jacob Andrew's great-great grandfather, became sheriff and served a two-year term. His son, William E. Andrew served from 1938 to 1946 and, following a four-year term by Saulsbury Sparks, served again from 1950 to 1961, dying of a heart attack in his office.William's son Louis C. Andrew served from 1961 to 1994, retiring when he was 70. His son, then-Deputy Charles Andrew, served as acting sheriff until Phil Brown was elected sheriff the following year.Back then, the sheriff and his family lived in the center section of what is now the Caroline County jail. Two wings were added to the large brick structure, but Charles Andrew remembers when the original section was home."I got to know a lot of inmates," he said.He recalls the night his "mother had a fit" when a naked woman was brought in by the state police."They had to come in the front door and walk down the hall which separated the living room and dining room directly back to that one-room office" at the back of the house, he said."I would have been seven or eight" years old, Charles Andrew said. "So, she made my father go to the commissioners, and that's when they put stairs on the side of the building to come in the outside door." "Back then, when my father started, he was only making $2,600 a year," he said. "They had to supply their own vehicle. The only thing the county gave them was a radio that went into their own private car." That center section of the current jail is called the Andrew Building today.Until 1994, both the sheriff's office and jail were under the jurisdiction of the sheriff, according to Charles Andrew. When Brown became sheriff, the county Department of Corrections was formed as a separate agency, and Charles Andrew served as the superintendent for 13 years, after serving in the sheriff's office for 20 years.Charles's son Jacob, now the fifth generation to serve in the sheriff's office, serves the county with almost 50 fellow deputies. After serving in the Air Force, Jacob Andrew joined the sheriff's office and has been on the job for 19 years. "I love it. I love my job," he said.The commemorative badge symbolizes not only his family's history of serving county citizens in the sheriff's office, but a long legacy of the office's commitment to public safety stretching back to the nation's founding.At the five points of the badge's star are a Revolutionary War soldier, the Caroline County Circuit Court building, the original courthouse before the renovations, the original sheriff's office on Gay Street, and the current office, completed in 2021 on Double Hills Road."One of the things that former Sheriff Randy Bounds wanted to do was have a wall of sheriff's (pictures)," Baker said."So I told him that Jake is going to fulfill that dream of his." The sheriff's office is seeking memorabilia from the public for a future museum or showcase. If you have any artifacts, photos or clippings you'd like to share, contact Lt. Jacob Andrew at 410-479-4124 or jandrew@carolinemd.org.

Sheriff Donnie Baker commissioned this commemorative badge for the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Joining current Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker, center, are former Sheriff Phil Brown, left, and Sheriff Randy Bounds.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
H. Saulsbury Sparks served as Caroline County Sheriff from 1934 to 1938, and again from 1942 to 1946. Note the handcuffs on his desktop.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Charles Andrew, left, served as acting sheriff and was a deputy for 20 years with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.

 The Easton Police Department announced its first Community Police Academy.The goal of this program, the department said in a press release, is to educate the public about the Easton Police Department and to increase the rapport between community members and police officers.The Community Police Academy will take place from 6 to 9 p.m. on the following eleven evenings: Jan. 17, Jan. 24, Jan. 31, Feb. 7, Feb. 15, Feb. 21, Feb. 28, March 6, March 13, March 20 and March 27.Most of the classes will meet at the Easton Police Department on 106 W.Dover St. in Easton. Class size is limited, so don't wait."Questions about this program can be directed to: EPDCareers@eastonmd.gov. title: Talbot Police Accountability Board Releases Inaugural Report
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot Police Accountability Board releases inaugural report

 January 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Police Accountability Board's first year was marked by challenges in adjusting to citizen oversight in policing, but "reluctant confidence" from law enforcement is believed to be growing, the board said in its inaugural report.The annual report, submitted to the Talbot County Council on Dec. 20, 2023, outlined the board's yearlong struggle in establishing a rapport with the county's four law enforcement agencies, which voiced concerns with the state-mandated legislation that created the board and a committee to review complaints of police misconduct.
Trends in call volume, arrests, struggles with recruitment and retention, use of force and police-community relations within each of the county's law enforcement agencies were analyzed in the report.
The board also asked the County Council to consider a number of recommendations to improve police accountability in Talbot County.
However, the board said most of the concerns from local police agencies centered on the Administrative Charging Committee, which is tasked with determining if officers should face administrative charges following a police agency's own investigation into the allegations. The committee also recommends appropriate discipline.
The committee is composed of five county residents and is helmed by Mitchell Ettinger, who also serves as the chairman of the Police Accountability Board.
Gaining the confidence of the county's law enforcement agencies proved to be the Administrative Charging Committee's great challenge last year, the report said.
Police questioned the wisdom of citizen oversight, the breadth of the committee's role and a lack of experience in law enforcement, which could translate to a gap in understanding the tasks and competing interests police officers face daily, according to the report.
In 2023, 15 complaints were submitted to the Administrative Charging Committee for review: 10 from the Sheriff's Office and five from the Easton Police Department.
Twelve complaints resulted in officer exonerations or were ruled as unfounded charges. Three complaints ended with varying disciplinary actions — two of which involved disagreements on recommended dispositions between the Administrative Charging Committee and the officers' respective agencies, the report said.
In one case, a Sheriff's Office deputy was administratively charged for undue use of force. According to the report, the deputy deployed pepper spray in an attempt to stop a juvenile who was improperly operating a mini-bike on the road.
The Administrative Charging Committee found it was unreasonable for the deputy to do so and imposed charges. The committee recommended two days' loss of pay, which the deputy accepted, according to the report.
The Sheriff's Office also revised its policy to clarify that deploying pepper spray on a moving motorist is inappropriate.
Use of force reports were a particular focus of the Police Accountability Board in 2023, according to its report. Law enforcement agencies now submit those reports quarterly.
The board's report said given the extensive interaction between police and the public, it was "remarkable" that officers only resorted to use of force on 10 occasions — six times by the sheriff's office, three times by the Easton Police Department and once by the St. Michaels Police Department.
Another case was heard against an Easton officer for unbecoming conduct off-duty, along with administrative failures to report conduct and a subpoena to testify. The allegations in that case were sustained, with the committee recommending two days' loss of pay or leave and a letter of reprimand.
The committee heard a third complaint against a sheriff's office deputy for speeding, which the deputy acknowledged. The deputy received a letter of reprimand.
Despite a year of building relationships, some distrust still lingers between the Administrative Charging Committee and local law enforcement.
"...The LEAs most certainly will maintain that they did not (and do not) need citizen oversight to exercise proper review and disposition of citizen complaints," the report said.
Though work remains to be done, the board believes the Administrative Charging Committee has established credibility with police through its "well-reasoned and supported" opinions on each of the complaints.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey acknowledged the lack of consensus between law enforcement and the committee on some case dispositions, but he said there was space for those disagreements.
"I think that we all want to be going in the same direction, and that is to have professional law enforcement in Talbot County," he said. "I've never gotten a sense from either entity, the PAB or the ACC, that they're looking to do in law enforcement like has been the narrative nationally for a few years of some groups — not all groups."
"We understand that it's important to have a rule of law in our community, and we just want it to be done well," Lowrey continued.

title: Oxford Police Chief Steps Down
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford police chief steps down

 January 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 438
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Oxford Police Chief Eric Kellner is stepping down from his position, but he will be staying with the Oxford Police Department.At a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Thursday, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said Kellner would be stepping down for "personal and professional reasons," but that he would stay on with the police department as an officer.
Kellner was not present at the meeting.
In an interview Friday, Kellner said he was grateful for the opportunity the commissioners gave him.
"This decision is both for personal and professional reasons and (is) in the best interest of the Town of Oxford and myself," he said. "But I look forward to continuing to serve the Town of Oxford in my new capacity as patrol officer."
Kellner, who took the position in April, said that being the police chief for Oxford was challenging and rewarding.
Regarding his new rank in the department, Kellner said he didn't think anything had been finalized and wouldn't be finalized until a permanent chief is appointed.
Until the town finds a permanent chief, Oxford Police Department's Lieutenant Chris Phillips will fill the role of interim chief. At the meeting Thursday, Lewis said the town will be posting a request for applications for a new chief, per employee hiring policy, "in the near future."
In an interview Friday, Lewis called Kellner a "phenomenal" officer and said she was happy he would be staying with the department.
"I'm happy to have three wonderful officers in our department," she said.
This change in leadership in the Oxford Police Department is the second change in about a year. In mid-February, the previous police chief, Patrick Maxwell, retired abruptly, leaving the department with just one officer. Maxwell had served in the town's police department for 34 years, spending 12 of those years as chief. The town did not provide a reason for his retirement.
In an interview, Phillips, who has been with the department for about five years now, said taking on the role of interim chief will be a challenge, but it is one he is looking forward to.
"I've been in the profession now for about 10 years, and it's something that I've strived towards," he said.
The challenge of the role, Phillips said, is something that comes with the territory of being in a leadership position.
"It's not something that I think should be taken lightly," he said.
As interim chief, Phillips' number one priority is consistency.
"Once the town is satisfied with finding the appropriate chief for the position, whether it be me or somebody else, then you can look towards more long term goals," he said. "But right now, it's just about public safety."
Reporter Natalie Jones contributed to this article.

title: Snow Fall Brings Snow Day on the Eastern Shore
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Snow fall brings snow day on the Eastern Shore

 January 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Residents woke up to two inches of snow Tuesday morning in Easton.With the snow came a snow day for Talbot County Public Schools students. Weather conditions caused the school system to close for the entire day.
Dorchester County Public Schools also closed for the day due to icy road conditions. Caroline County Public Schools closed for students, but offices opened at 10 a.m. for its 12-month employees.
Easton's Superintendent of Public Works Mike Dickerson said Easton Public Works used 46.92 tons of salt to keep the town's roadways safe. He said the department applied salt to the town's main roads — roads like Washington Street that get you into town — three times.
After receiving a notification from the Talbot County Department of Emergency Services, Easton Public Works began salting roads at 4 p.m. Monday. Dickerson said the last of the department's five trucks finished salting for the third time at 4:44 a.m. on Tuesday.
"We had five trucks out," he said. "And each one of them has an assigned route."
According to the National Weather Service, winter weather advisories for Queen Anne's, Talbot and Caroline counties were issued early Tuesday morning and in effect until 1 p.m. on Tuesday.
The advisories were for mixed precipitation with additional snow of up to an inch and ice accumulation of around one 10th of an inch. The advisories stated that morning commutes could be affected due to slippery road conditions.
Dorchester County received a winter weather advisory from the National Weather Service for freezing rain and additional ice accumulation. The advisory was in effect until 11 a.m. Tuesday morning.
As of noon on Tuesday, according to the National Weather Service, snow and freezing rain were likely in Easton before 1 p.m. with a chance of rain and snow between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. and a chance of more snow after 2 p.m. Little or no snow accumulation is expected. A tenth of an inch of ice accumulation is possible.
Dickerson said Easton Public Works has its trucks prepared in the event that employees have to go back out to take care of the roads.

title: Ridgely Suspends Entire Police Department

 The Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely Police Department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, according to a Wednesday release from the town.The commissioners are developing a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Department to guarantee uninterrupted public safety services for the Ridgely residents, the release said.
According to the Ridgely Police Department website, six officers are employed by the department.

Sheriff Donnie Baker said the Caroline County Sheriff's Department is ready to continue to provide services to the town of Ridgely.

title: Police Nab Theft Suspects Who Allegedly Stole $8K in Perfume from Ulta Store
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Police nab theft suspects who allegedly stole $8K in perfume from Ulta store

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 471

 Read News Document

 Five out-of-state individuals — four men and a woman — have been charged with felony theft following an alleged theft of nearly $8,000 worth of merchandise from Ulta Beauty in Prince Frederick.The incident occurred on April 4 at approximately 4:37 p.m., according to the Calvert County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to the store when a call went out that a theft had occurred.
According to a sheriff's office report, "Two males and one female entered the store and placed numerous colognes and perfumes into bags and fled the store. After fleeing the store, witnesses observed all three suspects enter a gray Mercury Montego that fled northbound on Route 4."
According to court documents filed by Deputy Antonio Tavares, Deputy Justin MacWilliams located the Mercury traveling northbound on Route 4, which then turned onto Route 2.
MacWilliams "initiated a traffic stop in the area of Pushaw Station Road in Sunderland. During the traffic stop, five occupants were located in the suspect vehicle along with numerous bags of perfumes and colognes in plain view. The total value of the stolen items was approximately $7,694 dollars."
In addition to the merchandise that was allegedly stolen from the Prince Frederick store, Tavares reported in charging papers that several cellphones were also confiscated.
The five arrested are identified as Yeiner Jose Rodriguez Barcelo, 27, of Bronx, N.Y., Yoncar Alberto Rainoso, 21, of Manhattan, N.Y., Estefani Andrea Urbano-Zapata, 21, of Cape Girardea, Mo., Raimil Marquez Jimenez, 25, of Washington, D.C., and Adony Josue Carana, 27, of Manhattan N.Y.
A sheriff's office press release stated that further investigation revealed Rodriguez-Barcelo was wanted on an open warrant from Pennsylvania for felony retail theft related to thefts at Ulta stores in Pennsylvania.
Court records show Carana, who was also listed with the alias Carrano, has been released after posting $10,000 bond. As of Monday, the other four remained at the Calvert detention center on a no-bond status.
A district court hearing on the charges the five are facing is scheduled for June 3. Language interpreters have been requested for four of the five defendants, court records show.
The Prince Frederick Ulta has been the scene of similar thefts over the last three years. Other Ulta stores regionally and nationally have been targets of alleged thieves. Several national news outlets have reported allegations of a possible retail theft ring in the state of California. The alleged perpetrators there stole $8 million in cosmetics from several chains, including Ulta, and then sold the products on Amazon.
It is not known at this time if the five arrested in Calvert last week are part of a larger theft ring.
Calvert County Sheriff Ricky Cox (R) issued a note of thanks in an agency press release to "the witnesses on scene that went above and beyond to promptly call 911 and provide details of the suspects and suspects' vehicle. Your efforts are greatly appreciated."

title: Commissioners Approve Extended MOU with Sheriff's Office for Ridgely Policing
author: Tom McCall
content:
Commissioners approve extended MOU with sheriff's office for Ridgely policing

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Building on a temporary agreement forged in the weeks following the March suspension of Ridgely's entire police force, the Town of Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have agreed to a more permanent plan for ensuring law enforcement coverage in the town.At their May 6 meeting, the Ridgely commissioners approved a memorandum of understanding for fiscal year 2025 that will ensure the sheriff's office provides law enforcement services to Ridgely in the absence of the Ridgely Police Department.
This is a longer term arrangement than originally conceived.
On March 13, the commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely police department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor. No reason for the investigation has been indicated publicly.
"To guarantee uninterrupted public safety services, the Commissioners initiated a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office," said Ridgely in a press release. "Now, building upon this temporary arrangement, Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have established a long-term partnership through an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). This MOU will provide the Town of Ridgely with complete law enforcement coverage, by the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, for the fiscal year 2025, with the option to renew service annually. This agreement includes a provision for maintaining 480 hours of coverage per month."
According to the first amendment to agreement for law enforcement services, a document between the town of Ridgely, the Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Sheriff Donald L. Baker, the estimated annual cost of this service is $474,971.44.
According to two versions of the town's proposed FY2025 budget, one with the town's police department and the other with the sheriff's office providing policing, posted to the town website Tuesday, the MOU with the sheriff's office cheaper the cost of maintaining a town police force.
"This partnership underscores our shared commitment to safety and community well-being," Baker said in the press release. "By working closely with the Ridgely community, we aim to build trust and ensure seamless law enforcement services to all residents. The updated MOU will take effect July 1, 2024, with the current MOU remaining in effect until then."
This matter was also addressed during the May 7 Caroline County Commissioners meeting.
"At this point in time, I plan on signing it if the County Commissioners sign it, and the (Ridgely) commissioners signed it last night," Baker said about the agreement at that meeting. "Frank Bartz was there. There was a lot of heated discussion, but that is to be expected. I look forward to the continued efforts by the county, the town and the sheriff's office. So I think that only good things are on the horizon."
Many Ridgely residents, like Lakia Harris-Pierce, who went to the meeting, are concerned about what they feel is a lack of transparency. Harris-Pierce said she is still wondering who gave the orders to suspend the police force in the first place.
Commissioner Larry Porter said, "I know there has been a lot of social media discussion about this, but basically this is going to provide 120 hours per week."
Then he asked the sheriff, "Just for clarification, how much coverage was the Ridgely Police Department providing when they were there?"
Baker said originally they were supposed to cover the town 140 hours a week. Vacancies and sickness kept them from reaching that number. The sheriff's office will cover the town as much as the police department had under the new agreement.
"Just so everybody knows, the sheriff's department is constitutionally obligated to handle and provide law enforcement services in Caroline County," Baker said. "Even if we back up the towns of Federalsburg, Greensboro or Denton, who have their own police departments… we are obligated to go in there… I do that in cooperation with the commissioners and your staff."
Baker said he takes the responsibility seriously and that he wants to give the citizens of Ridgely some peace of mind.
The county commissioners' motion unanimously passed to approve the MOU.

title: Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Starting July 8, police in Delaware will use electronic speed cameras to help enforce speed limits in the Interstate 95 construction zone near Del. 896 in Newark.The first three weeks will be a warning period. After the warning period, registered vehicle owners receiving a first offense will receive a base violation of $20, plus an additional amount for each mile per hour over the posted work zone speed limit of 55 mph.
For example, if the captured violation occurs at a speed of 66 mph, the speed violation is $20 plus an additional $11, which accounts for $1 for each mile per hour over the speed limit. Additional fees and court costs that are tacked on to all speeding tickets in Delaware will bring the total cost up to $118.
Second and subsequent offenses are higher. These violations are civil penalties only, and no points will be assessed to drivers' licenses.
State officials first announced the program in April, saying the cameras are an important tool to make work zones safer.
"Even though we've reduced the speed limits out here in the work zone, we're still seeing people speeding through there," Delaware Department of Transportation Secretary Nicole Majeski said at the time. "It is a tight configuration, so law enforcement has difficulty pulling people over. We've also seen a spike in crashes, so we're hoping the cameras will help."
Similar to the red light cameras common throughout the state, speed cameras will take pictures of violators' license plates, and those drivers will receive a ticket in the mail. The driver must exceed the speed limit by at least 11 mph in order to receive a ticket via a speed camera.
DelDOT first used speed cameras in 2022 when the state legislature authorized a pilot program focused on an I-95 project in Wilmington.
"We saw speeds reduced significantly, both northbound and southbound, and accidents were cut in half," Majeski said. "We saw as a direct result of having those cameras that people slow down, and it really paid off."
Last year, after lobbying from Newark officials and others, the legislature expanded the program to allow cameras in work zones and residential areas throughout the state. After developing regulations and choosing a vendor, DelDOT is ready to install the first new cameras in the work zone at the I-95/Del. 896 interchange, which is in the midst of a two-year reconstruction project.
Brandon Zerilla, who is leading the project for DelDOT contractor Wagman, said earlier this year that the cameras will be a welcomed safety tool for his workers.
"These cameras have proven to reduce the speeds in the work zone, reduce crashes and increase awareness in the work zone," Zerilla said, adding that far too many drivers do not slow down while passing through the I-95 construction site.
The interchange project, which is the largest work zone in Delaware, involves building new flyover ramps from southbound Del. 896 to northbound I-95 and from southbound I-95 to southbound Del. 896. The flyovers will increase the distance between exit and entrance ramps, reducing the traffic weaving that causes crashes at the current interchange.
The project also includes widening a one-mile stretch of the interstate to provide for longer acceleration and deceleration lanes, as well as upgraded lighting, rehabilitation of 10 existing bridges, the construction of six new bridges for the flyovers, and the construction of a walking and biking bridge over the interstate.
Work began last spring and will continue through fall 2025.

title: Talbot County Enacts Burn Ban
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County enacts burn ban

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 271
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON – Talbot County Council enacted a burn ban Friday afternoon as a heat wave makes its way through Maryland and local fire departments are seeing increased activity.Council members held a special meeting Friday to discuss the burn ban, which prohibits all "open-air burning." It will last for 30 days, until July 21, unless another resolution is passed to end or extend the ban.
A county press release defined open-air burning as "burning any material in the open or in a receptacle other than a furnace, … including use of fireworks, sparklers, or sparkling devices."
Backyard fire pits are also prohibited. Gas grills and propane stoves are allowed.
Sonny Jones, fire chief for Easton Volunteer Fire Department, has seen increased calls in the county during this spell of hot and dry weather.
"Right now it's so dry, just something as simple as a spark coming from a vehicle … or an ember that flies from someone who has a burn that they're watching, … can spread very, very rapidly," Jones said.
As the Fourth of July holiday approaches, Chris Robertson, state fire supervisor for the Maryland Forest Service, recommends all residents wait for rain before burning. He said county burn bans will help reduce dangerous usage of fireworks and sparklers.
"In Maryland, fireworks are pretty much limited to ground-based fireworks," Robertson said. "So hopefully there won't be too much of that. We do usually have some issues with fireworks, but not a great deal."
Somerset County and Wicomico County both enacted burn bans Thursday. In Talbot, public officers may enter private or public property to put out a fire and confiscate fireworks or sparklers during the ban.

title: Talbot County Passes 1-Cent Resolution for 2024 Ballot
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County passes 1-cent resolution for 2024 ballot

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Voters in Talbot County will see a familiar question on November's ballot.The Talbot County Council passed a resolution Tuesday to place a question on the 2024 ballot to amend the county's charter to raise residents' taxes for public safety.
The amendment would allow, but not require, the council to add up to 1 cent per $100 of assessed value above the revenue cap for an additional seven years beginning July 1, 2026.
After the council passed a similar 1-cent resolution in 2020, a majority of Talbot County voters in the 2020 general election approved the charter amendment.
Martha Sparks, the county's finance director, said the 1-cent resolution has allowed the county to add 26 public safety positions, including paramedics, EMTs, school resource officers and 911 operators. County Manager Clay Stamp vouched for the 1-cent resolution funding.
"In the last number of years, this additional funding has allowed us to see the best of our services," said Stamp, who is also the county's former emergency services director. "We've stabilized our workforce. We've been able to attract quality individuals as paramedics, correctional officers, deputy sheriffs. We've enhanced our technology, we've enhanced our coverage."
The original resolution from 2020 amended the charter for five years up until July 1, 2026. Resolution 359, which was passed Tuesday, adds an additional seven years.
Originally, Resolution 359 was introduced as extending five years. Council Vice President Pete Lesher proposed an amendment Tuesday to tack on the two additional years.
His reasoning for the amendment was to ensure any future extensions can be voted on by the public during presidential elections, when the ballot is more "uncrowded" than other elections. County council and gubernatorial elections are set to be in 2026 and 2030, meaning that if extended to only 2031, the 1-cent question may have appeared on a crowded 2030 ballot.
"By adding another two years, rather than having this expire in a council election year (or) a gubernatorial election year, this will extend it to the next presidential election year so that should this need to be renewed another time, it can be done when there isn't such a crowded ballot," Lesher said.
Council members unanimously approved the amendment 4-0 before passing the resolution by the same vote, with Council Member Dave Stepp absent.
Sparks said she's seen where the additional tax revenue has been spent, which is in "the areas that the public has supported," noting the new positions and increased funding to volunteer fire departments.
"It's very important for the public to know that they're doing good things to help us," Council President Chuck Callahan said.

title: Ridgely Residents Call for Police Department to be Reinstated
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely residents call for police department to be reinstated

 August 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Following tense public comment at Monday's Ridgely Town Meeting, residents are calling for the Ridgely Police Department and its officers to be reinstated after nearly five months of suspension.The Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the department in March, with pay, pending an investigation by the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor. At Monday's meeting, residents raised that the department and its officers had been exonerated by investigators surfaced.
Multiple people asked for the department to be reinstated. Resident James Romph questioned the commissioners and town employees on the investigation.
"What is the update on the Ridgely Police Department investigation?" Romph asked.
"Sir, I'd love to answer that but I was told to keep my mouth shut," David Crist, the town's director of public works, responded.
"I'm going to answer it for you, for the public," Romph said. "The entire police department has been exonerated. The state has concluded their investigation and found no fault with the police department or the police chief, criminally or administratively. They're exonerated."
As of Tuesday, town employees and the Office of the State Prosecutor did not immediately respond to requests regarding the report and whether or not it cleared the department and its officers.
Romph claimed the commissioners had "known for over two weeks and didn't share that with you," speaking to the standing-room-only crowd, which included members of the police department.
"No we have not, we have not been notified," Commissioner John Hurley said. Crist backed the commissioners up, saying they hadn't been notified but confirming that he had been. Romph questioned why Crist did not inform the commissioners or the public.
"From my counsel, I was told this is a personnel matter, you cannot speak," Crist said. "I'm not a lawyer, I don't know law. But if the town attorney tells me to zip it, I'm zipping it."
Since the initial suspension, the town has not provided clear reasoning for the investigation. Nor has the Office of the State Prosecutor.
The town came to a temporary memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, agreeing that the Sheriff's Office and Maryland State Police would split duties to cover the suspended department.
In May, the town agreed to a new memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, this one providing a "long-term partnership" for fiscal year 2025. It included "a provision for maintaining 480 hours of coverage per month," per a town release, and took effect on July 1.
Caroline County Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer told The Star Democrat on Tuesday that the updated MOU is still in effect. As of Tuesday, the county had not heard from the town requesting to cease the MOU. Such a request would require 30 days of notice, Helmer said.
Residents have brought concerns about the county's law enforcement coverage compared to what town police provided. Resident and business owner Holly Justice says it hasn't been the same.
"When you deal with a big giant, you lose a lot of those small-town things," Justice said in an interview. "The county, they have a lot of area to cover, and although we have officers that they did dedicate to this territory, it's just not the same."
Justice created a petition Tuesday, asking the town to reinstate the officers. As of Tuesday evening, it had over 30 signatures.
"People's lives were jeopardized with this," Justice said. " … These people have families. My heart goes out to them. But I also understand the town's side, being told by their counsel that they can not speak about this matter.
"Instead of joining in with the brigade and yelling and fussing, I said, 'What's a better way to come at this? What's a better way to be heard and be seen?'"
Resident Lakia Harris-Pierce said she believes residents should be informed on the investigation's results. "They need to make the investigation public, we have the right to know," she said.
Town commissioners are meeting in closed session Wednesday afternoon to discuss personnel matters, according to an agenda posted to the town's website.
Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado and Tom McCall contributed reporting to this story.

title: Down to One Officer, Greensboro Considers Closing Police Department
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Down to one officer, Greensboro considers closing police department

 September 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 592
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The future of the Greensboro Police Department is up in the air.Mayor David Spencer announced at Thursday evening's Greensboro Town Council meeting that the town will consider closing its police department, which is now down to one officer, Chief Lenox Trams.
Four options were provided to the mayor and commissioners by Town Manager Tammy Kelledes:
Continuing running its own police department.Working "in conjunction with" the Caroline County Sheriff's Office "to fill the spots (it doesn't) have now for (its) own officers."Entering into a "contractual agreement" with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.Closing the police department, not entering into an agreement and turning "the town over to the sheriff's department and the Maryland State Police."
"The current public safety demands are too much for a one-person police department to handle," Spencer said. "In addition, the mayor and council must consider the increasing costs of retaining a police department and the struggles caused by a shortage of police officers and police applicants throughout the state."
"We will listen to all comments and suggestions and take all of those into consideration," he added. "We will not be making a decision tonight."
The mayor emphasized Thursday was just the beginning of a "fluid" and long-term process.
Greensboro has been receiving assistance from county police in recent weeks to reduce the burden on the town's only officer. Spencer said Greensboro has been paying a $75-per-hour rate for county deputies to cover the town, which will continue "in the meantime."
"When they come in here, they're staying here," Spencer said. "They're not patrolling the county, they're only patrolling the town."
A person recently hired by the town did not complete police academy training, Spencer said in response to a resident question.
Spencer said the town has asked Trams to continue going through officer applications on file in hopes that an applicant who is already certified can be brought on board. Otherwise, certification and training can take up to a full year.
"If you put somebody through the academy, it takes about a year," Trams said. "When you hire them after you do the background, for the nine months that they really aren't much good to you, you are paying their salary and their health insurance."
During his department update, Trams urged those with non-emergencies to call the county at 410-479-2515 since the Greensboro department is limited. "If (we're) working, they will certainly send us. If we're not working, then they will send the next agency that is in rotation," he said.
PUBLIC FEEDBACKAfter Spencer read the four options aloud, resident Paula Turner pushed for more details and asked for the town to host a special meeting.
"Of those options, where is the breakdown of cost, of savings?" Turner asked "If No. 4 is voted in, if that's what the town wants, show us how … (the) money that's budgeted will be allocated back into our town. I want numbers."
Kevin Parks spoke in support of the police department remaining. He referenced the struggle to attract police officers due to Maryland's repeal of the Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights back in 2021.
"I don't want to see the police department closed up," Parks said. "The chief's doing the best he can. If you want to fuss about the police department, call your legislators and your senators for the state of Maryland and tell them to give them their bill of rights back."
Spencer said the town's budget has room for three officers. Public Works Supervisor Brandon Cunningham asked if the town would continue paying for county assistance if it hired a second officer only.
"Those decisions have not yet been made," Spencer said.

title: Everbridge Becomes Kent's New Emergency Alert System
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Everbridge becomes Kent's new emergency alert system

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Even at 3 a.m. from his home, with a tap of a button Emergency Preparedness Planner Brian Pearsall can send out an alert to a majority of Kent County residents.He hopes he never has to do that, but it's beneficial the option's there.
In the basement of the Kent County Sheriff's Office, where the Office of Emergency Services is housed, he demonstrates how efficient he can be in sending notifications with the department's new software, Everbridge.
On July 1, they made the switch from their old system Code Red, a commendable program in its own right.
Why the switch?
"It allows us to be more effective to the community with updated information regarding weather forecasts and gives us a larger environment to do that with their technology," Pearsall said.
Pearsall explained there are three levels of communication.
Everbridge is a TSP level 3 certification, designated Public Health, and receives restoration priority just under Federal government certifications. It is required to be backed up and restored in order to provide for public health.
He pointed out, Everbridge is used widely throughout the state right now making communicating between counties convenient.
"We can coordinate better as far as resource needs," Pearsall said.
Everbridge can target specific areas within the county as well.
In a simulation, a test, on his cell phone, Pearsall uses the map on the Everbridge application to send out a storm warning to just Kennedyville residents.
Narrowing it down even further, if needed, he could send notifications to just a specific housing community within Kennedyville.
These alerts are available to residents who have phones in a contract with Everbridge. But also residents can receive specific notifications by signing up to receive alerts at https://www.kentcounty.com/oes.
Those who sign up get alerts for weather conditions, tornados, flash floods, and even water line repairs and other infrastructure information.
So far, the new software has gone off without a hitch as they've sent out 10 alerts since the time of the interview in late August.
Along with other administrators, Director Pete Landon and Chief of Communications Brad Russum, Pearsall meets regularly over Zoom with the Everbridge team to increase their knowledge of technology which always seems to be adapting.
The emergency team is always looking to learn as much as they can to increase the public's awareness and safety.
Like for example, in a few months time they will be able to provide IPAUS, Integrated Public Alert and Warning System.
"When you receive an amber alert on your phone, you can't stop that from coming through. So soon I'll be able to provide this to our residents and visitors," Pearsall remarked.
In the case of an impending tornado for example, he can interrupt every phone in Kent County warning residents.
He's been taking FEMA courses online, and when the time comes, will take an exam for certification along with quarterly tests.
The team's also looking to expand public's awareness like the recent Maryland Mesonet Weather Station, set up at the back of the A.F. Whitsitt Center. It's one of 70 weather stations in the state in partnership with the University of Maryland, Maryland Department of Emergency Management, Maryland Environmental Service and Maryland Department of Health.
These stations are spaced about 10 miles apart and solar powered, measuring rainfall, snow, even the temperature of the top soil.
"It has all manner of capabilities and allows us to be more effective in predicting and forecasting weather events," Pearsall added.
Like the Everbridge program, the station provides opportunities to cooperate with various local, state and federal entities.
All these expansions are part of an effort, "To create a safer Kent County by getting the resources to the community, residents and visitors."

title: Cambridge City Council Extends Juvenile Curfew Another Year
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council extends juvenile curfew another year

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a four-to-one vote on Sept. 9, the Cambridge City Council extended its temporary juvenile curfew for another 12 months.The curfew — which was originally passed in September 2023 — makes it so that juveniles under 16 cannot be in a public place within the city between the hours of 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. on Sundays through Thursdays and 11 p.m. through 5 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.
There are exceptions to this, including when the juvenile is with a parent or when the juvenile is on the way home from work or a school activity.
The extension will keep the curfew in place through Sept. 30, 2025.
At the City Council meeting on Sept. 9, a public hearing was held before the commissioners took a vote. Resident Shay Lewis-Sisco, who is running for Cambridge's Ward 2 commissioner seat, said that during a community visioning session at Mace's Lane Middle School, most of the students involved said they were in favor of the curfew.
Commissioner Sputty Cephas brought up a conversation he had with one young person. He said the curfew made the child think twice about going out at night.
Cephas, who voted to extend the curfew, asked the other commissioners whether they thought the curfew should be reviewed annually or on a longer-term basis.
Commissioners Jameson Harrington, Brian Roche and Laurel Atkiss all said they think the curfew should be reviewed on an annual basis.
Harrington, who voted against the extension, said an annual review allows the council to more easily end the curfew if it isn't working.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Harrington said he voted against the curfew as a principle. He said he has been against it from the start and data shows it is not effective, but he said he is proud of how it is working in Cambridge.
Roche and Atkiss both spoke about the curfew's effectiveness in allowing Cambridge Police to have conversations with children and employ community policing.
"But definitely an annual reevaluation is great because we hope to make progress and maybe not need such structures at some point in the future," Atkiss said.
Before the vote, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said he thinks the curfew is a good tool. He said there has been less juvenile crime during the hours of the curfew compared to 2023 "when it was a real crisis." He said the curfew has made children think twice about going out at night and has allowed the department to reach more children.
At the end of the meeting, Todd thanked the council.
"I just want to thank everyone for the support of the curfew and the continuation of it for another year," he said. "It's much appreciated."

title: Caroline Commissioners Talk New Regional Detention Center
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners talk new regional detention center

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Oct. 15 the Caroline County Commissioners discussed a plan to build a new regional detention center in Queen Anne's county.The financial burden would be split between Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties, but it is still unclear how that would be managed or what would happen to the detention center on 101 Gay Street in Denton, commissioners said at the meeting.
The new facility is being designed to hold 338 beds for men and women. The current Denton jail holds 130 inmates.
The warden of the Caroline County Detention Center, Charles Scott, said there are mental health needs among the inmates that could be better managed with a designated space, which could be incorporated into the design of the new facility.
"There should be a wing just for mental health. Juveniles and mental health are just piling up in the jail," Scott said.
He said there is plenty of land in Queen Anne's County to build this new detention center. The new facility will be located in Church Hill on the site of the Eastern Pre-Release Unit.
Commission President Travis Breeding cited the economies of scale and how the new detention center could serve the needs of the counties for less money.
The commissioners discussed who would be the authority on this tri-county project. Right now, one county commissioner and one county administrator oversee the jail in Denton. The commissioners said they wanted more clarity on how that would work in a tri-county context.
The commissioners also discussed the employment possibilities for current Caroline County Detention Center employees. Employment decisions would factor in tenure and managing workers who have fulfilled this amount of time as they work in a new county.
Scott said it is hard to find correctional officers, so everyone's job should be safe.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the new facility will offer better services at lower costs, but the devil is in the details.
The commissioners agreed to discuss this further at the next meeting on Oct. 22 at the Health and Public Services building.

title: Talbot County Places Burn Ban
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County places burn ban

 October 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 244
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council has enacted a burn ban as a dry spell has rendered the county without rain for weeks.Council members held a special meeting Friday morning to pass the burn ban, which prohibits all "open-air burning." Effective Friday, it will last for 30 days, unless it is extended or terminated.
A county press release defined open-air burning as "burning any material in the open or in a receptacle other than a furnace, … including use of fireworks, sparklers, or sparkling devices."
Brian LeCates, county director of emergency services, said in a memorandum to the county that the request for a burn ban came from volunteer fire chiefs. The county's burn ban committee requested the council enact the 30-day ban.
"Their concern is that we have had abnormally dry conditions with no appreciable precipitation in the weather forecast," LeCates wrote.
LeCates noted that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is "currently classifying Talbot County as having abnormally dry conditions."
"Looking at our weather forecast, we do not show any significant precipitation in the near future," he wrote. "The Maryland Department of Natural Resources Forest Service has listed our area as highly susceptible to fire due to these conditions."
Last week, Dorchester and Wicomico counties each enacted burn bans due to drought-like conditions. On Oct. 22, Wicomico County voted to extend its burn ban.
Talbot County most recently enacted a burn ban on July 21, which was placed due to similar dry conditions and a significant heat wave.

title: Counties and Towns Prepare for Snow on the Mid-Shore This Weekend
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties and towns prepare for snow on the Mid-Shore this weekend

 January 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With snow in the forecast this Sunday and Monday, Mid-Shore towns and counties are making plans and readying their snow plows."Every storm is different and unique," Easton Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said. "But we feel that we're prepared and ready for the storm."
On Friday, the Talbot County Department of Emergency Services had a meeting with local towns to coordinate in preparation for the winter weather.
According to the National Weather Service forecast as of Friday afternoon, snow is likely to fall in Easton from Sunday night into Monday. The weather organization is expecting a "major winter storm" will bring snow and ice across the country, "from the Central Plains to the Mid-Atlantic" this weekend.
Sunday night, there is a 90% chance of precipitation in Easton with snow expected mainly after 1 a.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Monday, there is a 90% chance of precipitation in Easton with snow expected before 1 p.m. and then rain and snow likely. Monday night, there is a 50% chance of precipitation.
Talbot County Public Schools Communications Director Debbie Gardner said the district is monitoring the forecast to determine if closures will be necessary.
Dorchester County Emergency Management Division Director Jimmy Windsor said Dorchester County has warned all its departments of the predicted weather, including its Highway Division. He said the county's Highway Division is preparing its inclement weather plans.
Van Emburgh said on Friday that Easton was putting plows on the fronts of trucks and loading salt into the trucks that spread salt.
"And we have equipment that we're placing around town that we'll use to address alleys and some of the tighter spots that we plow," he said.
Windsor said it is important that residents make sure they take the usual winter preparedness precautions, such as making sure vehicles have gas in them. He said that residents who live in areas that are prone to power outages should make sure they have blankets and warm clothing in the event of an outage.
"And a supply of fresh water in case the power goes out and you're on well water and therefore you rely on the power for your water source," he said.
Van Emburgh said it's helpful if residents do not park their cars on main streets.
"When people park on the streets, we have to plow around the cars and sometimes that can — depending on how much snow we get — that can get tricky and then we plow the cars in," he said.
Van Emburgh also talked about the importance of not plowing snow from the sidewalks into the street.
"Because we then plow it back onto the sidewalk," he said, laughing. "It's just a battle. (Residents) plow it onto the street. We plow it back onto the sidewalk. And they get mad at us."
Van Emburgh said residents should plow snow off their sidewalks by starting in the center of the street and working toward a house or building so that the snow is plowed into a yard.
"Some properties don't have yards," he said. "But if you plow it out in the street, it's just going to get pushed back onto the sidewalk. So we ask that everything moves away from the center of the street."

title: Gasser Plans to Take Federalsburg Police in the Right Direction
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Gasser plans to take Federalsburg police in the right direction

 January 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 539
 Words

 FEDERALSBURG — Joseph Gasser has taken his new role of chief of police in stride, setting goals to help further the Federalsburg Police Department amid turnover and a third-party investigation.On Wednesday, Gasser was publicly named chief of police in a Facebook post made by the town government. Gasser has been interim chief of police since October, when an unspecified incident caused the town to have a third party investigate the department.
Gasser comes into this position with a military background, and he has been serving the Town of Federalsburg for almost 30 years. He believes his strong background and experience will help him serve as chief.
"The jobs that I have had throughout both my military and my police career have pointed me in this direction," Gasser said. "As not somebody simply to have a standard to take over, but someone that has the ability and the knowledge to build from."
On Oct. 14 the Town of Federalsburg made a facebook post about an unspecified incident causing the town to have a third party investigate the department.
"The Town of Federalsburg received a complaint about an incident involving the Federalsburg Police Department that occurred on October 9, 2024. We are engaging an independent third party to investigate this incident," the post said.
When asked whether turnover in the Federalsburg Police Department was related to the October incident, Mayor Kim Abner referred the Star Democrat to the Facebook post.
Gasser confirmed the October incident was a consideration in his appointment. "But that's as far as I'll go with it," he said.
In the post announcing Gasser promotion, the town stated former Chief Michael McDermott, who had served in law enforcement for more than 40 years, resigned effective Jan. 5.
"The Mayor and Council, on behalf of the Town of Federalsburg, extend our appreciation to Chief McDermott for his years of service to the Town and wish him all the best in his future endeavors," the town said in the Facebook post.
In McDermott's years as chief, the department saw a significant reduction in crime rates, the post said. Gasser wants to continue McDermott's work.
"We've had a good several years here with the former chief, and I want to expound upon that and make it even better for the future," Gasser said.
Some of Gasser's goals and plans will be executed within three years, the new chief said. He plans to shape the department better for the future.
"We have several new officers with less than a year in the field," Gasser stated. "They are the future of this department. My primary goal is to prepare this department three years down the line, five years down the line, for those individuals to take over this department and to run it effectively and in service of the community."
In addition to continuing the work that has been done, Gasser plans for some reorganization as well.
"There's certainly some internal reorganization to the department that needs to be done," Gasser said. "That's going to be a transitional point, both with me coming in as Chief, even though I've been here forever. It's also going to be a task to better serve the officers themselves, like some officers have things they like to do more than others, I want to get them headed in that direction."
