title: Cambridge Sees Reduction in Crime in 2024 Compared to Previous Year
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge sees reduction in crime in 2024 compared to previous year

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 529
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge saw a 14% reduction in crime in 2024.While presenting the Cambridge Police Department's 2024 year end report to the Cambridge City Council on Jan. 27, Police Chief Justin Todd called this accomplishment the "big one."
He said the department achieved many accomplishments in 2024.
"I have a lot of people to thank for that," he said. "Not only my officers and the staff, but also the city staff and the commissioners." Todd said it wouldn't have been possible without funding and the "numerous resources" the department was provided.
Along with reducing crime overall, Todd mentioned increasing the number of cameras around the city, creating better working relationships with the Dorchester County Board of Education and the Department of Juvenile Services and reaching a clearance rate of 69.6% in the department's Criminal Investigations Division.
Todd said the average clearance rate, which is the rate of crimes that are solved, is around 28% nationally. "So that just shows you what a good job they are doing," Todd said.
Todd also talked about the department's efforts to map crimes by where and when they occur. He said that informs how the department spends its time patrolling.
"We make sure that officers are in those areas as much as possible during that time," he said.
Todd listed the department's continued commitment to community-oriented policing as an accomplishment.
"These things, patrolling with purpose and community-oriented policing, will continue as we charge harder to fine-tune it and make it better," he said.
When it comes to specific crime stats for 2024, there were 30 aggravated assaults reported. Todd pointed out the "significant difference" from 2022 when there were 110 aggravated assaults reported in Cambridge. Compared to 2023, there was a 53% reduction in aggravated assaults in Cambridge in 2024.
According to the report, compared to 2023, burglaries and simple assaults were down 12% and 16%, respectively, in 2024.
Todd said that like 2023, there were two homicides in Cambridge in 2024. This number is a decrease from seven homicides in 2022.
Todd said one of the homicides in Cambridge this year was the result of gun violence and the other was a kidnapping in Easton that law enforcement officials believe resulted in a homicide in Cambridge.
The number of robberies as well as the number of rapes and sex offenses each increased by 12% in 2024 compared to the previous year. Todd said some of those rape and sex offenses investigations are still open.
RECRUITMENT AND RETENTIONDuring his presentation to the City Council, Todd also talked about the city's efforts to recruit and keep a full staff, which will continue into 2025.
"We're going to recruit, recruit, recruit good quality people that want to invest in the City of Cambridge and be here," he said.
Todd said the city has 36 sworn officers, including a civilian liaison officer. He said they were ready to put three people in the police academy but one didn't make the final interview and the other two determined it wasn't a good fit.
"So we're back at the drawing boards," he said.
Todd said the department has seven civilian employees.
"That has been significant in helping us do our daily work and customer service as we continue to move along," he said.

title: Easton Police Chief: Traffic Stops Bill Would Have 'Drastic' Impacts on Police Work
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Police Chief Alan Lowrey raised concerns over a proposed bill in the state legislature that would limit police officers' abilities to make traffic stops for certain violations.Senate Bill 292, cross-filed in the House of Delegates, would shift many primary offenses to secondary offenses, including improper use of headlights and taillights, failing to use turn signals, missing or improper license plates, and excessive noise.
That change would mean police officers can only cite a driver for those offenses if they pull over the driver for a different, primary offense.
During an Easton Town Council meeting Monday, Lowrey, also serving as the interim town manager, said the bill's proposed changes would be "drastic" and negatively impact police in detecting crime.
"There's a number of concerns on my part as the chief of police, and I've spoken with my staff about this," Lowrey said.
Lowrey said offenses such as driving without headlights are common signs indicating potential impaired driving. He said all of the offenses that would be reclassified are safety issues.
"I personally have arrested a number of people, based upon traffic stops, for serious crimes," Lowrey said.
As written, the bill seeks to make evidence gathered during traffic stops inadmissible if an officer fails to state their name, identification number, agency and reason for the stop. Lowrey called that measure "drastic" as well.
Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) is the bill's sponsor. At a Jan. 28 Senate Judicial Proceedings hearing, Sydnor noted Baltimore County statistics that indicated Black and Hispanic drivers face inequities in the rate of citations issued.
"It is these disparities that spurred me to seek and introduce a legislative remedy," Sydnor said.
Sydnor said he worked with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender on the drafted bill. Moving primary violations to fall under secondary violations make way for technologies such as cameras to detect traffic violations, the senator said.
"Technology that can be modified to do what people do today," Sydnor said. "So really, this bill kicks off a conversation about, I would say, a reimagining of how we deal with traffic offenses on the highways."
At the hearing, though, some legislators and law enforcement officials from around the state spoke unfavorably of the legislation.
Those conversations around Maryland have continued in the weeks since. Last month, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed the bill at a meeting and expressed intent to write a letter in opposition.
Monday in Easton, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said the job of being a police officer is "tough enough as it is."
"We don't need to make it any tougher," Abbatiello said. "So I would support anything that the town would like to do in order to try to prevent this from passing."
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Lowrey how the town could express its concerns regarding the bill. Lowrey suggested drafting a letter.
Following discussion, Easton councilmembers voted unanimously to send correspondence to committees in Annapolis opposing the bill.

title: Ridgely Commissioners, Residents Weigh in on Potential of Reinstating Police Department
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ridgely commissioners, residents weigh in on potential of reinstating police department

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Over a year after suspending the now-defunct Ridgely Police Department, town commissioners say reestablishing the force will cost the town nearly double its projected payment to the county sheriff for police coverage.At a workshop Wednesday, Commissioner Brad Sears told residents that restoring the department would cost an estimated $852,000. Ridgely currently receives dedicated coverage from the Caroline County Sheriff's Office based on a memorandum of understanding. Renewing that MOU for fiscal year 2026 would cost $493,000, per estimates.
A number of residents questioned the Town Council's openness to consider reinstating the department. Concerns raised stem back to the town's controversial decision to suspend and subsequently lay off the department last year amid a criminal investigation into the police chief that came up empty.
Residents were only permitted to testify in front of the commissioners Wednesday if they had signed up around a day in advance.
Heather Amador said the workshop felt like the town was "checking a box."
"I feel solid that your minds are made up," Amador told commissioners. "Some of you openly expressed that at the last town meeting. It feels pretty certain that my words and efforts will be for nothing."
"We're not going to make any decisions tonight," Sears said. "We're not really going to take questions, because we want to focus on what you, the public, have to say. And we want to take some time to properly consider what you have to say."
The commissioners suspended former Police Chief Jeff Eckrich and the entire department March 12, 2024, amid a state criminal investigation into Eckrich due to "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office.
On July 25, 2024, an investigation report by the Office of the State Prosecutor found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution."
But by that time, the Ridgely officers had already been laid off with the start of the new fiscal year July 1. The town began selling and transferring its police vehicles and equipment in the weeks before the state prosecutor's report was released.
Since then, Ridgely has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town. Last week, the Sheriff's Office announced a third officer was assigned to the Ridgely patrol group.
At Wednesday's meeting, Sears explained why Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker and Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer weren't in attendance.
"They wanted to attend, but they were advised by their attorney not to attend because there is potential litigation outstanding," Sears said. Lt. George Paugh attended in their place.
While two residents submitted written testimony in support of maintaining Caroline County Sheriff's Office coverage, residents who spoke at the meeting largely asked for two other options: reinstating the town's force or ending the Sheriff's Office contract and operating like towns such as Goldsboro and Preston, which receive general county and state police patrol.
"Since the sheriff has taken over, we've had no community policing like before," said Christine Eckrich, wife of the former Ridgely chief. "And a lot of the hours have not been covered. So now my question is, what are we paying for? Why are we double paying for the Sheriff's Office to come to Ridgely."
Resident Anna Mansfield questioned if the budget estimates for a reestablished town force and the county coverage are comparable.
"Was the Ridgely Police Department afforded the ability to reduce their hours to meet the amount of hours expected for the desired budget?" Mansfield asked commissioners.
Sears, who assumed his seat in July 2024 after the department's suspension earlier that year, prepared the cost estimates by reviewing past police budgets, meeting with a consultant and comparing projections to other local departments.
He said it's key to have "rationale and cost effective reasons" when considering creating a police department.
Resident Jennifer Nesselroad stood up to express her displeasure.
"We had a police department, and we don't need to start a new one because you illegally took ours away," she said, leaving the room.
President John Buckle said in an opening statement that "the commissioners will listen carefully to what everyone has to say." Commissioner John Hurley provided no comment at the workshop.
As the meeting closed, Sears emphasized that reinstating the police department would require infrastructure and safety improvements to the department's office within the town hall building.
"But the police department existed how many years without those features," resident Robin Martin said.
"Things have changed a lot over the last five to 10 years," Sears responded. "The racial incidents, the general degradation of respect for authority, COVID and so on has changed our cultural landscape. Violence is on the upswing."
"It's very difficult to be a police officer," he later added. "It's very difficult to attract and retain police officers."

title: Police Accountability Legislation Worked on by Caroline County Commissioners
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Police accountability legislation worked on by Caroline County Commissioners

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners conducted the second reading and public hearing for a legislative bill making changes to legislation defining the county's Police Accountability Board, Administrative Charging Committee and trial boards.The changes come after law enforcement agencies voiced confusion about how far the powers of these boards and committees extend.
"I will tell you in practice that (law enforcement agencies) have to work with the ACC. This has to be a partnership. This should not be a combative relationship," Executive Director of Police Training and Standards Commission Wayne Silver said.
The committees and boards were formed as a result of the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021, which aimed to create a system for evaluating and investigation complaints against law enforcement agencies.
The county implemented the accountability board, charging committee and trial boards when required by the state. But the exact duties and appearances of these boards are still being fine-tuned through the county's legislative processes.
Silver talked with the county commissioners about the trends seen in other counties and about how these counties implemented the boards and committees.
One of the questions presented by the commissioners asked about the subpoena power of the charging committee. Silver gave insight on how subpoena power should be implemented.
"To my knowledge, Caroline County is the only county to ever subpoena an officer," Silver said. "The ACC does not have subpoena authority... Our position on this, ladies and gentlemen, is that it is the law enforcement agency that would issue the subpoena if it was necessary."
In December, law enforcement officials from multiple counties gathered at a Caroline County Commissioners meeting, bringing concerns about an incident involving a Caroline County sheriff's deputy and its implications for police accountability practices throughout the state.
The deputy, who was not named, was investigated by the administrative charging committee about a harassment complaint. Committee members invited the deputy to meet with the committee regarding the complaint, a move considered by some sheriff's departments to be "not proper protocol" or an "overreach."
After a 40-minute conversation with Silver on Tuesday, the commissioners opened the public comment period for the legislative bill.
While no one spoke during the public comment period, the county received multiple letters from the Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee and a letter from Denton Chief of Police George Bacorn on behalf of other chiefs in Caroline County.
After discussion, some of the important changes made within the legislative bill establishing the roles and powers of the boards include:
Clarifying definitions and language and correcting grammar errors.Adjusting requirements of board members, including removing the three-year residency requirement and allowing members to attend meetings virtually. The commissioners will also appoint an alternate member of the Police Accountability Board.Removing subpoena language from the legislation. The ACC recommended paragraph removal on subpoena responsibilities, but commissioners decided to the remove "subpoenas" sentence from the paragraph.

title: Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 262
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A Newark park will be closed for the foreseeable future after a recent inspection found "significant safety concerns and hazardous conditions," city officials said.One of the city's lesser-known parks, Coleman Park is located near the Maryland border, bounded by Valley Road and the Country Hills and Briarcreek neighborhoods. The main entrance is in Country Hills.
The 8.5-acre park contains walking trails but otherwise is preserved in its natural state.
The inspection found that the tree canopy near the entrance to the park consists of many black locust trees that are structurally compromised by fungal decay and pose a significant risk of falling.
The walking paths are eroded and surrounded by dense thickets of greenbrier, multiflora rose and poison ivy.
"These thorny species have overgrown the area and become entangled with large woody debris from fallen trees and limbs," City Manager Tom Coleman wrote in a memo to city council. "Significant land clearing and tree removal must be completed before we can reopen the park."
The city does not have funding for such work in the 2025 budget, according to Coleman, who did not provide any indication as to when the park might reopen.
The city's five-year capital improvement plan includes plans for broader improvements to Coleman Park, such as building a turf/meadow area, planting new trees and possibly paving the trails. However that $50,000 in funding, which is dependent on a state grant, is not budgeted until 2027.
Coleman Park was created in 1993 when Newark purchased the land for $180,000 and annexed it into the city. It is named for the family that previously owned the property.

title: Trappe Volunteer Fire Company Seeks Funding for Firehouse
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Trappe Volunteer Fire Company seeks funding for firehouse

 July 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 396

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company is raising funds to build an up-to-date firehouse. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md. 1st) wants to secure federal funding to help.The Trappe Volunteer Firehouse was completed in 1951 and has not been updated since. "We probably have the oldest one in the county," Assistant Secretary Treasurer of the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company Cheryl Lewis said.
Lewis said a new firehouse is necessary because the current building is no longer suitable for the modern equipment.
Because Trappe has a volunteer fire company, like many towns on the Eastern Shore, projects like this rely heavily on government and local support, Lewis said.
"We've been in the process of trying to get assistance," Lewis said. "In the last budget year, the federal budget that was just approved, we had successfully worked with Andy Harris's office to be included in the budget. But with the cuts that were done early on this year, it was removed."
Harris said the appropriations bill to provide funding for the project failed due to negotiations in Congress leading to a continued delay, but she said the project has been reapplied for in the current year's legislation.
"We hope the appropriations process has a better outcome, but then that's not up to us because it involves the minority party as well," he said in an interview with the Star Democrat.
In order to qualify for federal grants, the company must match 25% of the projected project cost of $6 million. The company set a goal of $1,500,000 and set aside $450,000 to begin the efforts.
Fundraising efforts include The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company's upcoming annual fair, held on July 31 through Aug. 2 at the firehouse. The event begins at 6 p.m. and ends at 10 p.m. each day and will include fire truck rides, hay rides, food, games and prizes, and live entertainment, according to the fire company's Facebook page. Saturday's event will open with a parade.
Harris said the outcome of federal funding depends on the successful bipartisan negotiations in Congress to pass this version of the appropriations bill.
"In the end, this is going to depend on the minority party. And you know, if they're not willing to negotiate in good faith, that could end up being a problem," Harris said. "The people in Trappe have to know that their member of Congress was working hard to get that money to the fire company."

Federalsburg police chief resigns; sheriff's office takes over leadership

 FEDERALSBURG — At the July 7 town meeting, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner announced Police Chief Joseph Gasser resigned from his position on June 25."The mayor and council would like to announce the resignation of Chief Gasser from the Federalsburg Police Department effective June 25," Abner said. "We want to thank Chief Gasser for his service to the town and wish him well on his future endeavors."
Within the announcement, Abner said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would take over leadership of the Federalsburg Police Department to give the mayor and council time to figure out police department leadership.
"I was contacted by the mayor and council and asked to take over day-to-day operations and management oversight of the department," Sheriff Donald Baker said to the Star Democrat in an interview Tuesday. "I agree to do that on an interim basis for 30 to 60 days until the mayor and council decide what they are going to do moving forward and what that looks like for the Federalsburg Police Department."
The mayor also announced a public forum meeting for July 21 at 6 p.m. at the Federalsburg Town Hall to discuss their options moving forward with the police department, public safety and policing.
While the sheriff's office and the town of Federalsburg are in the early stages of conversation, Baker believes all options are on the table for the Federalsburg Police Department, including an memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office that could discontinue the police department.
"I believe that everything is on the table to include signing an MOU somewhat like Ridgley's, directly with the sheriff's office of the county," Baker said. "Again, everything is on the table. and we are really early in this stage, but we absolutely could absorb any officers that were left."
Gasser was appointed to police chief position in January. He came into the position with a military background, and he had been serving the Town of Federalsburg for almost 30 years.
Ridgley has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town since last year. In March 2024, the town suspended its police department amid a state investigation.
More recently, Ridgley has agreed to continue the memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office for the next fiscal year.

 An incident that led to a man's arrest in June 2024 resulted in a five-count indictment this summer from a Calvert County grand jury.The defendant is identified in court papers as Edward Dewey Viens Jr., 39, of Laurel.
According to court documents, on June 5, 2024, deputies from the county's sheriff's office were initially sent to the Huntingtown area in response to a missing person report. The deputies were then dispatched to CalvertHealth Medical Center after it was learned the 32-year-old woman who had been reported missing had been located.
Viens was also at the hospital, investigators reported.
In charging papers filed by Deputy Ryan Gough, the woman claimed she had been held against her will by Viens, who was her boyfriend at the time.
Gough said Viens' accuser had bruises on her face, lacerations on her arms, neck, hands and legs, which were the result of an alleged assault by the defendant. That assault reportedly occurred while the two were riding in Viens' truck.
Gough stated in court documents that the woman told him Viens exhibited strange behavior during the ride and kept insisting the truck was being followed. She said at one point she tried to flee the truck, which led to Viens assaulting her.
Another sheriff's officer, Detective Thomas Buckler III, confirmed Viens was making strange remarks about being followed.
A search of Viens yielded four packages of suspected Suboxone.
The July 21 indictment charges Viens with one count each of kidnapping, first-degree assault, second-degree assault, possession of contraband in a place of confinement and false imprisonment.
Viens initial circuit court appearance was Monday before Judge Andrew S. Rappaport.
A pre-trial conference is scheduled for late August with a plea hearing scheduled for late September.
Prosecution of the case will be handled by Anthony R. Navalaney of the Calvert County State's Attorney's Office.
Viens is being represented by the public defenders office.

title: CPS Staff Under Investigation in Caroline County
author: Lily Tierney
content:
CPS staff under investigation in Caroline County

 August 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Caroline 
 
 746
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An investigation into the work of Caroline County Child Protective Services is long overdue, county Sheriff Donnie Baker said.The internal investigation into CPS staff was prompted by an incident on July 13, where a social worker never arrived to a home where child abuse and neglect was reported, according to Baker.
He said the agency has been "lacking in their responses," including showing up over an hour after being called or not responding to calls of abuse or neglect until law enforcement has already handled the situation.
"There are some issues that the local Caroline County Department of Social Services needs to work out, and we have been working with them for quite some time to work out," Baker said.
The state Department of Human Services is conducting the internal investigation. Maryland State Police are investigating the report of abuse and neglect.
Baker and Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin met with the secretary of Human Services about a year ago to address long CPS response times.
"We were promised a lot of changes, and unfortunately, those changes have not come to fruition," Baker said.
The Caroline County Department of Social Services, which oversees CPS, did not respond to requests for comment.
Ben Shnider, director of communications for the state Department of Human Services, which oversees the Caroline County department, wrote in an email to the Star Democrat, "The safety and well-being of Maryland's children is our highest priority, and local departments of social services respond to every report of alleged child abuse or neglect."
According to Department of Human Services policy, the Caroline County Child Protective Services response times fall within the guidelines for responding to reports for the examples that Baker cited.
The policy calls for:
Answering calls of physical or sexual abuse within 24 hours.Answering calls for reports of neglect within five calendar days.Answering calls for cases of substance-exposed newborns within 48 hours.
But Baker and Franklin said this policy leaves law enforcement to act as a middle man, but addressing the problem is complicated.
The Caroline County Department of Social Services is a state-run agency over which the county has no control, making it difficult for local agencies and officials to affect change, Franklin said.
"I have no power to enforce changes, I can only make recommendations," Franklin said.
Baker and Franklin said there have been unfulfilled promises of solutions since the problems began during the pandemic but were vague as to what those problems and promises were, saying they wanted to preserve their working relationships with CPS.
Both said they want a better working relationship with Child Protective Services. State law mandates law enforcement agencies working with CPS.
After-hours reports of child neglect or abuse can be handled in a few different ways. In cases involving high or even moderate risks, a Child Protective Services case worker should be automatically dispatched, but if they cannot respond, law enforcement, generally the sheriff's office, will be sent.
Because of the mandated joint investigations, Baker said law enforcement officers have been picking up the slack when the case workers do not arrive, leading to increased frustration by the officers on the scene.
Part of the problem may be vacancies in the state Department of Human Services, where there is a 7% vacancy rate, although Baker said he thinks the root cause stems from procedural and cultural issues that start with upper management.
"I would say that everything starts from upper management and works its way down as far as a cultural issue," he said. "And I think that there are some procedural issues within the agency itself."
Baker spent a majority of his career working in child abuse investigations and said they are near and dear to his heart.
"I know how hard that is, so it's very disheartening to me when we do not have good partners," Baker said.
Shnider, the Department of Human Services communications director, said his agency "is committed to holding ourselves accountable." His email statement said the department will address any systemic issues that are identified through the investigation.
"Any failure to respond to a report of abuse or neglect in a timely manner is unacceptable," Shnider said. "When mistakes are made, we hold ourselves accountable and take action to ensure we do better moving forward."
In the meantime, Baker and Franklin hope the investigation will bring systemic change that will enhance their partnerships and the safety of the children in Caroline County.
"I hope that some accountability and changes will come to better protect the kids," Franklin said.
This report has been updated to clarify that MSP and DHS are conducting separate investigations.

title: Ex-Officers Sue Ridgely, Sheriff Over Disbanding Force
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ex-officers sue Ridgely, sheriff over disbanding force

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Push 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Former Ridgely police officers have filed a lawsuit against the town and Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker, claiming the defendants "orchestrated a coup" to disband the now-defunct Ridgely Police Department.The lawsuit was filed Aug. 13 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland by seven former officers, including former Police Chief Jeff Eckrich, and a civilian employee. Named as defendants are Baker, Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer, current and former town officials and a former Ridgely officer, as well as the State of Maryland and the Town of Ridgely.
The lawsuit includes 13 counts, claiming the defendants violated due process and the 14th Amendment, committed civil conspiracy and committed defamation.
One count claims the Ridgely Town Commissioners at the time — John Hurley, John Buckle and Anthony Casey — wrongfully discharged the police officers. Hurley is an active commissioner; Casey resigned in June 2024 and Buckle lost a reelection bid in April.
Baker declined to comment on the lawsuit when reached Tuesday evening, citing legal advice. Patrick Thomas, an attorney for the Town of Ridgely, wrote in an email that he can't "comment on pending litigation involving" clients.
Eckrich and former police department employees ask for the town to pay economic damages for lost wages and benefits, among other items. Plaintiffs are also seeking the court to demand the town reinstate its department and employees.
In March 2024, Ridgely commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department with pay pending an investigation by the state prosecutor. At the time, the town didn't indicate reasons for the investigation.
At a closed session meeting in April, the town laid off the dismissed officers and support staff, a move that took effect July 1, 2024.
Later that July, the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor released a report in which it investigated Eckrich for "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office. The report found "no sufficient evidence" of the alleged criminal activity, closing its investigation into Eckrich.
Other officers were not investigated in that state prosecutor's report.
In September 2024, Ridgely commissioners stuck by their plans not to reinstate the police department despite heavy criticism from residents at town meetings.
By that time, the town had already sold police vehicles and equipment to nearby agencies, including the Caroline County Sheriff's Office. Those transactions were made in the days leading up to and following July 1, 2024, the effective date the officers were laid off.
The lawsuit alleges that the investigation by the Office of the State Prosecutor was based on allegations made by former Ridgely police officer James Joles, also named as a defendant. Joles, according to the lawsuit, blamed Eckrich for his threatened termination from the Ridgely force in January 2024 that led Joles to resign from the department.
The lawsuit claims Joles met with Baker, the sheriff, "and the two devised a plan that would eliminate the RPD and allow Sheriff's Office to assume responsibility for law enforcement in the Town of Ridgely."
The town has been under contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office for police coverage since. Currently, three county officers are dedicated to Ridgely patrol.
This May, the town opted to continue its memorandum of understanding with the Sheriff's Office, agreeing to pay $493,000 for policing services, according to the town's fiscal year 2026 budget.
This story has been updated to clarify the plaintiffs and defendant listed in the lawsuit. As of Sept. 2, this story has been updated to correct John Buckle's title as a former Ridgely commissioner.

title: Body Cam Video Released of Cambridge Officer-Involved Shooting
author: Staff Report
content:
Body cam video released of Cambridge officer-involved shooting

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Dorchester 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — A man who was shot and killed by a Cambridge police officer asked the officer to shoot him as he charged the officer with a knife.On Thursday evening, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General released the body-worn camera footage from the fatal officer-involved shooting that occurred Sept. 4 in Cambridge.
The preliminary investigation released in the days following the incident revealed Jacob Weber, a corporal from the Cambridge Police Department, fatally shot 30-year-old Ryan Garcy of Cambridge after Garcy charged at Weber with a knife.
The nine-minute video released by the attorney general's office includes footage from the body-worn cameras of three police officers — Weber and two officers identified only as "witness officer from the Cambridge Police Department."
The footage shows an exchange between Weber and Garcy that lasted under a minute.
During the interaction, Weber repeatedly tells Garcy to drop the knife he is holding and to stay back. Garcy, who was naked, can be seen slowly approaching Weber's police vehicle before pausing and asking Weber, "Will you just f------ shoot me?"
Garcy can then be seen rapidly approaching Weber. Weber is seen deploying a Taser, which is ineffective, then running from Garcy before firing five shots in Garcy's direction.
"I can say that I'm very proud of the officer that, from what I see, with all his training and knowledge of the job, he did what he, unfortunately, had to do to survive, and that's about all I can say about that for now," Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said Friday.
Garcy was transported by Maryland State Police Aviation to Tidal Health Peninsula Regional Medical Center in Salisbury, where he later died.
Weber, who has been with the police department for six years, has been placed on paid administrative leave until the investigation by the attorney general's office is finished, Todd said.
According to Todd, this is Cambridge's first fatal police shooting in about 15 years.
"I can say my condolences for the family of Mr. Garcy having to go through that and have that video out there. I can't imagine the pain and heartache," Todd said. "Mental health is a real problem."
Todd said he has been in contact with Garcy's family via email since the incident and considers the experience traumatic for both the family and the officers involved.
"We all sign up to do this job, and yes, we know it can come to that, but I don't think anyone can speak for it until you actually have been through something like that," Todd said.
Todd does not know when the investigation from the independent investigations division will conclude, but he said the investigators have been in touch and have been great to work with.

title: In Wake of Fatal Hit-and-Run, Route 50 Safety in Easton a Concern
author: Konner Metz
content:
In wake of fatal hit-and-run, Route 50 safety in Easton a concern

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 826
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Safety concerns for pedestrians and bikers using Route 50 in Easton are being raised after a fatal hit-and-run crash Saturday.Donald Dawson, a 68-year-old Easton resident, was killed riding a bike early Saturday morning in what police said was a hit-and-run crash with a box truck or tractor trailer. Police are still searching for the suspect vehicle.
The crash occurred at U.S. Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
On Monday, Town Council President Don Abbatiello implored residents to drive safely.
"We already have enough people who come through town speeding. We don't need to add to that," Abbatiello said.
The fatal crash occurred just north of the Immanuel Lutheran Church and across from Saints Peter & Paul High School. Slightly north of the crash location is an overhead sign instruction drivers of the traffic light ahead, reading: "urban area stay alert." The speed limit reduces to 45 mph as drivers funnel toward the Route 50 and Dutchmans Lane intersection.
Saturday's crash is the second fatal collision on that stretch of road this year. In February, a car struck and killed a 35-year-old man near Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
In response to questions about Route 50 safety in Easton, State Highway Administration spokesman Danny Allman said pedestrian activity near Woodridge Drive "is not encouraged as there are no sidewalks nor shoulders" on that side of the highway.
"We always emphasize visibility for pedestrians and cyclists on any road," Allman wrote in an email statement Tuesday. "Pedestrians and cyclists should always wear reflective apparel, especially in areas with no separation or lighting."
Saturday's fatal crash is also raising the question of whether speed cameras should be placed along Route 50 in Easton. Abbatiello said the cameras are needed.
"I also am pleading with the state to consider adding speed cameras on Route 50," he said during Monday's meeting. "We are talking about adding two crosswalks, one at Dover, one at Goldsborough, hopefully within the next year. We're going to have people walking across Route 50. It needs to be safe for them to do so. And so I hope that the state will seriously consider a request for a speed camera on Route 50."
Easton has its own speed enforcement program to deter speeding in school zones. School zone signs with "photo enforced" written under them indicate where the cameras may be active.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said speed cameras on town streets and roads have been successful. There are cameras near the YMCA and The Country School, he said.
"I think that speed cameras help change behavior," Van Emburgh said.
While Saturday's crash didn't occur on a town-operated road, Easton engineers are in communication with their counterparts at the state level, he said.
Allman said SHA doesn't have "enabling legislation" to install speed cameras in non-work zones. Per state law, jurisdictions can install cameras in school zones and sometimes residential and other areas, he said.
For a camera to be placed on a state route, Allman said a jurisdiction would have to submit a request to SHA and receive a permit to place the camera.
Abbatiello said in an interview Tuesday that the next step for the town to consider requesting a speed camera permit for Route 50. The precedent is already set in Salisbury Abbatiello noted, pointing to speed cameras on the highway near Wicomico Middle School.
"It's a real issue in Easton," Abbatiello said of Route 50 safety.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey said on Wednesday that the police department is working with a speed camera vendor to assess safety on the highway. "There's a lot of work to be done" before officially submitting a speed camera request to SHA, Lowrey said. Work includes gathering crash data.
"The goal is safety, the goal's not revenue," Lowrey said. "That's how the state looks at it, too."
According to SHA, sidewalks and pedestrian crossings are in the works for two Route 50 intersections — Dover and Matthewstown Roads, or Routes 331 and 328, respectively. Construction will begin in early- to mid-2026, Allman said Tuesday.
For roads maintained by the town, a draft comprehensive "Complete Streets" study is expected to be presented to town officials in the coming weeks. It will outline target speed limits, assess the need for sidewalks or bike lanes and, overall, put "safety first," Van Emburgh said.
"It's gonna tell us what we want our roads to look like," he said.
Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit that advocates for pedestrian and bicycle safety, said in a statement on Monday that the town's Complete Streets study and similar safety efforts by Talbot County officials are important.
"These efforts need to be, at their core, about saving lives," the statement read.
Talbot Thrive's statement also addressed Saturday's fatal crash.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the vulnerability of those who travel by foot, bicycle, or wheelchair in our community — and of the urgent need to make Talbot County's roads safer and more connected for everyone, not just for those in cars," the statement read.

author: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com, njones@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg elects first two Black council members in historic election

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com, njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 814
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG - Just under 300 voters braved a gray and drizzly Tuesday to cast their ballots in Federalsburg's bicentennial election, making history in electing two Black women to the town council.While the election falling during the bicentennial year is special on its own, the day was historic for a different reason - it was the first election held under the town's recently passed election plan, and it was the first time a Black resident had been elected to the town council in the town's 200-year history.According to Kristy Marshall, Federalsburg's interim town manager, 283 residents voted in Tuesday's election, accounting for 17% of the town's registered voters.The mayoral seat and all four council seats - two council members for each newly created district - were up for election.Incumbent Mayor Kimberly Abner held her position at the helm of the town, earning 191 votes and a five-year term as mayor. Jeffrey Stevenson, Jr., a first-time candidate, received 83 votes.In the newly created District 1, which has a majority Black population, representation was achieved for Black residents with the election of two Black women to the council seats.Darlene Hammond received the highest number of ballots, earning 70 votes and a five-year term on the town council.Brandy James received 52 votes, earning a three-year term on the council.James held a narrow lead over incumbent councilman Scott Phillips, who received 49 votes.In District 2, only two candidates - Debra Sewell and H. Torbert "Toby" Williamson - ran for the two open council spots, locking in their seats on the council even before the election.Sewell received 135 votes, earning a five-year term. Williamson received 90 votes and a three-year council term.The new election plan, passed in June, changed the town's former at-large, staggered term election system to a two-district system that ensured more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents.No Black resident had ever been elected as a mayor or council member in the town's 200-year history until Tuesday's election.The change was spurred by a federal lawsuit filed earlier this year, which contended that the former election system discriminated against Black voters by keeping them from being able to elect their chosen representatives.Abner, who has served as Federalsburg's mayor since 2019, faced a challenge from Stevenson, a lifelong town resident who hoped to bring change, leadership and caring for the future of the community.To Abner, time already served as an elected official mattered."People look at experience and pay attention," she said.Paying the town's debt, fixing pump stations and paving roads are also among Abner's priorities.When asked why he was running, Stevenson gave a simple answer: "If not me, then who?" "Man, I always felt like I was a leader, and I was always willing to take the chances that everybody else won't take," he said."I'm getting older now, so I've had interest in politics because it matters to me now - I pay taxes, I'm invested in the city - so it's like the things that I wasn't concerned about as a child, as a man coming of age."For James, a 25-year Federalsburg resident and first-time candidate, choosing to step up and run for one of the District 1 council seats came from a simple question she asked herself, "Why not?" "It was more so like, 'Will I be here for another 25 years and just continue to complain and nag about things that need to be done, or will I be that person that tries to be a part of the change - you know, be the change you want to see," she said.To James, changing the town's level of transparency with residents is a major factor, especially when it comes to ensuring that the community knows what the town is doing, whether it's a municipal election or roadwork."I want to make sure that the information that is conveyed is information that is understood by anybody on any education level, like you shouldn't have to have a master's or doctorate degree to understand what they're talking about," she said. "I just want to make sure that it's plain and simple and understood."On a similar note, James said the town should publish relevant information in both Spanish and Creole to serve Federalsburg's Hispanic and Haitian populations.For Federalsburg's Black residents, the first election under the new plan is one they've long been waiting for."I appreciate everybody that (would) listen to me, that listened to my cry, and took interest in doing what they've done to get this," said Roberta Butler."It took a while, it took awhile - can you imagine, 200 years? That's a long time." 
 
 Caption: Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner, left, poses for a photo with incumbent Councilwoman Debra Sewell, who ran in District 2 to preserve her seat.
 
Federalsburg resident Roberta Butler spoke of the election in biblical terms. She said finally, someone had heard her cry after 200 years.

title: Settlement Calls for Apology, Restorative Measures in Federalsburg Voting Rights Case
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Settlement calls for apology, restorative measures in Federalsburg voting rights case

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 921
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Plaintiffs in a historic lawsuit against Federalsburg this week reached a $260,000 settlement that includes an apology to the town's Black residents and other requirements memorializing the case.At a table in the newly opened Harlem's Kitchen restaurant in Federalsburg, two Black residents of the town, Roberta Butler and Jeff Stevenson Jr., sat down Friday to discuss shifts in their hometown.
Much of the change in Federalsburg is visible. On Sept. 26, the town elected its first two Black council members, a result of the lawsuit leading to the town's settlement with the Caroline County branch of the NAACP, the Caucus of African American Leaders and Federalsburg residents regarding its discriminatory election system.
"It's a work in progress," Butler said. "But I think we will get there."
The settlement is seen by many as not only a step forward for Federalsburg, but for the nation.
The conversation between the two Federalsburg residents echoed those happening throughout the town. Butler said Federalsburg's historically Black community is happy about the settlement.
For Butler, who was a plaintiff in the lawsuit, it's about the future generations. She said her grandchildren are "very excited" and added that if you talked with her granddaughter, her granddaughter would say "'My mom mom is doing this for me."
"I'm proud of all my grandkids," Butler said. "I'm doing it for them."
Stevenson, who was not named in the lawsuit but who ran for mayor in the September election, said a lot of the town's Black residents just want to see change.
"We just hope that they take us (seriously)," he said.
The April 1 settlement includes a sweeping array of measures aimed at providing reconciliation after Federalsburg's previous at-large election system was determined to have prevented Black residents from electing their chosen representatives.
The town's Black population has grown steadily over the years, with Black residents now accounting for about 43% of the roughly 2,800-resident population.
But until last September, the town had never had Black representatives on the Town Council in its 200-year history.
The settlement came just over a year after the plaintiffs filed suit in federal court in Baltimore under the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Through months of charter amendments, legislation and federal court rulings, the town's previous at-large election system was changed in June to a two-district system to ensure more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents. District 1 has a 64% Black population and District 2 is predominantly white.
Two Black women were elected to the Town Council during Federalsburg's Sept. 26 election — Darlene Pitt Hammond and Brandy James.
The settlement calls for a total of $260,000 in legal fees to be paid by the town to the American Civil Liberties Union of Maryland Foundation. Within 30 days of the agreement, $50,000 to be paid to the ACLU, then $35,000 every October between 2025 and 2030.
Under the settlement, the town will be required to:
Deliver an official signed and written apology addressed to those who brought the lawsuit. This apology will be framed and posed permanently in Federalsburg's town hall.
Affix a plaque "marking the town's voting rights victory brought about through the contributions of the Plaintiffs in this case" to the town hall building.
Create a photo display in conjunction with the historical society and the plaintiffs featuring Black community contributions to the town, which will be displayed at town hall.
Rename Gerardi Boulevard to Brooklyn Avenue.
Erect a historical marker in the town's Black community of Brooklyn celebrating the contributions of the neighborhood's residents and their ancestors.
Proclaim Sept. 26 as Voting Rights Day in recognition of Black voters' historic win on that date in 2023.
Create a town committee to focus on community engagement in future elections and matters related to the promotion, engagement and enhancement of the town's diverse community. At least one elected town official and two community members from each election district will serve on the committee.
Establish an annual multicultural celebration for the town.
"The Town of Federalsburg formally acknowledges responsibility and expresses its deep regret for actions and inactions contributing to racial discrimination and exclusion of Black residents, including its use of an election system that prevented any Black person from holding a position on the Town Council over 200 years," reads the town's written apology. "As officials of the Town, we accept moral accountability for the harms these actions inflicted upon Black residents, their families, and ancestors before them."
Carl Snowden, convener of the Caucus of African American Leaders, said that in his more than 30 years of involvement in voting rights cases, he has never before seen a municipality willing to admit its wrongs and apologize for it.
He said this "historic landmark decision" is bigger than Federalsburg.
"What Federalsburg has done is become a model to what can happen throughout Maryland and the rest of the nation," he said.
Snowden said he will use Federalsburg as a model in other cases the caucus takes on.
Willie Woods, president of the Caroline County branch of the NAACP called the settlement rewarding.
She said they are focusing on what has been accomplished and plan to build on that success moving forward.
"Build on the foundation that's been put in place," Woods said.
An event to celebrate the settlement is in the works.
"There's a degree of optimism when you have achieved something you worked hard for and you wondered if it would come to pass," Woods said. "And to see that that has happened — Yes, that's going to be a major celebration."
Since the settlement, Butler has been thinking about her parents, grandparents and other Black Federalsburg residents that are no longer alive.
"I just wish my ancestors could have seen this," she said.

title: LGBTQ community sees fear, persecution in Easton
author: RUDY REYES
content:
LGBTQ community sees fear, persecution in Easton

 June 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: RUDY REYES | Section: Columns 
 
 733
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "We the people," the words that begin the Constitution are words that refer to us, all of us. The Declaration of Independence states we are all created equal. Not some people: all of us. We are a free people in a land we love and cherish, who should live without fear of persecution for being who we are.But unfortunately, we have seen the Republican Party promote fear and persecution against the LGBTQ community, and it has reared its ugly head in our town. The queer community in Easton and Talbot County at large is a strong, vocal and diverse community that has always been here. It's not a new phenomenon, we didn't just come out of nowhere.
Only recently have we shown how proud we are and appreciate the sacrifices that have been made by those who came before with Delmarva pride. But some on the Easton Town Council see us as a threat.
Our esteemed Town Council President, Frank Gunsallus, and Councilman David Montgomery seem to believe that the freedom of expression by the LGBTQ community here in Easton, granted by the Constitution, is abhorrent, not only to themselves but also to society.
We as a community are not "a socialist endeavor" as the council president asserted. Councilman Montgomery said on June 3, "I did not hear a single word in our last meeting that in any way constituted an attack or a slur on any individual person who is lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans-sexual, queer or anything else." Yet he uttered in the same breath, "We were discussing, first an issue about the town, displaying Pride flags, and that I would simply say that I do not believe it is the town's business to make everyone feel good about their identity."
If that's the case, then you could make an argument about other town events like Waterfowl, St. Patrick's Day parade, Christmas parade, Fourth of July festivities, and the art and ice sculpture festivals. These events, you could say, make people "feel good about their identity," whether a Christian celebrating Christmas, someone of Irish heritage, an artist, a resident of the shore, or even as an American.
Gunsallus failed to mention any other "ideological group" he would disfavor, further proving his deliberate attack on gay pride. At the crux of the uproar is his proposed legislation to prohibit the expenditure of county funds to support "ideologies." He proposes it as a measure merely aimed at fiscal responsibility. Ironically, it is fiscally irresponsible, as the measure would jeopardize annual events that bring revenue to the town. This is first a discrimination issue for the town, but also an economic issue.
This isn't a game. Pride is and was meant first as a protest, fighting for the same basic rights that heterosexual people enjoy.
I will always remember the six words displayed on the town council dais in which the council sits: "Trustworthiness, Respect, Responsibility, Fairness, Caring and Citizenship." I question if this council is upholding these principles that are the foundation of our town.
Can Easton citizens now feel they can trust the council to represent these values? Councilman Montgomery and council President Gunsallus don't seem to care about or respect the people who have opened their hearts inclusively to all who visit Easton.
We, as a community, stand united against this latest insult by two of the town council members. Fortunately, the council does not speak as one voice on this issue. Mayor Megan Cook, council members Maureen Curry, Don Abbatiello and the Rev. Elmer Davis, who constitute a majority of the council, spoke for themselves and made their support for the LGBTQ community clear. This speaks volumes. I know that their support is appreciated.
If President Gunsallus dares to bring up for a vote this measure that he proposes, I hope it will be resoundingly defeated.
Gunsallus will serve as council president until April 2025. We don't know if he will run for re-election. I implore all residents of Easton to remember this sorry incident during the campaign for election of the next council president.
Will the new council president uphold the values of the town inscribed on their dais? Do we want more political fights and controversy that divide us? Or do we want someone who will stand up for us all and protect the values Easton purports to uphold? I leave you with that choice.
Rudy Reyes is a resident of Easton and a member of the Talbot County Democratic Forum.

title: Memorial Proposed to Recognize US Colored Troops in QA
author: Niambi Davis Special to the Bay Times Record Observer
content:
Memorial proposed to recognize US Colored Troops in QA

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: NIAMBI DAVIS Special to the Bay Times Record Observer | Section: News 
 
 723
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — For many years, Chris Pupke, past president of the Queen Anne's County Historical Society and advisory board member of the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center, has shared his knowledge of the county's African American history with the community through a series of lectures. His talks on the county's United States Colored Troops veterans, those enslaved and free men who gave their service and lives to the Union Army during the Civil War, have honored descendants and enhanced public knowledge of the County's diverse history.On Aug. 13, joined by veteran's representative Jim Barnett; fine artist and charter Captain Tilghman Hemsley, and Marcia Landskroener, Pupke presented a proposal to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners for the creation of a statue to honor the county's USCT veterans.
Accompanied by visual aids, his presentation featured the regiments and military campaigns in which Queen Anne's County free and enslaved men courageously served. In describing the invaluable service of the nation's USCT veterans, Abraham Lincoln proclaimed that "without the military help of the black freedmen, the war against the South could not have been won."
More than 120 Queen Anne's County men fought with the 39th USCT in the Battle of the Crater, part of the July 1864 Siege of Petersburg. They were trained to lead the attack until a last-minute change proved to be disastrous. When the USCT were sent in to salvage the operation, they discovered the mission was lost. "But they stood fast. These heroes stood in reserve, ready to do their duty, to honor their oath to the country, for which they paid a dear price," Pupke declared.
James Bond of Centreville, described as a "mulatto", was enslaved by Dr. James Bordley of Centreville. Bond enlisted on December 17, 1863 and was immediately made a sergeant. Sgt. Bond may have been among the casualties of the Battle of the Crater.
In the fall of 1863, more than 125 men from Queen Anne's County enlisted in the 7th USCT Regiment. The fight took them to the barrier islands from Hilton Head to Jacksonville. "You know these men were brave," Pupke told the audience of commissioners and interested citizens. "If you've ever walked the beach and seen the movie Glory, it was that kind of fight."
Particularly poignant was the recollection by Colonel James Shaw of the September 1864 Battle of Chaffin's Farm: "Not a man faltered, but all who did not fall reached the work, charged boldly, and did all in their power to take it….they are all missing."
Before Queen Anne's County's Robert Riley enlisted in Company B, 7th USCT Regiment, he had been enslaved on the Wye River. His Pension File included a surgeon's note of "scars of whip on back when a slave." But as a USCT soldier, Private Riley was present at the Battle of Fort Gilmer and among his fellow African American troops at Lee's surrender at the Appomattox Courthouse. Riley is buried in Chesterfield Cemetery in Centreville.
To honor these men who fought for their freedom and for their country, a group of veterans approached Tilghman Hemsley with the idea of creating a statue in their memory. "I thought it was a very worthy idea," he stated. After walking the grounds of the Courthouse, Hemsley believed the best placement for the monument would be set in the same promenade as the memorial honoring county POWs; "not a large monument but certainly worthy of their service." The inscription would include the quote by Abraham Lincoln with the USCT story engraved in granite. Hemsley shared concept drawings of the proposed statue with completion for the monument expected for 2025, the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
On Sept. 7, from 5-7 p.m., the Queen Anne's County Historical Society will host a free fall picnic at Wright's Chance, 119 S. Commerce Street in Centreville. This event replaces the July event which was postponed due to the intense heat experienced throughout the entire month. Pupke will discuss Queen Anne's County USCT history. Kay Brown, a member of Bryan's United Methodist Church, will share church history and the success of Bryan's United Methodist Church in preserving a significant piece of Queen Anne's County history. This opportunity was provided by a grant awarded to the church by the Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture and the Maryland Historical Trust's African American Heritage Preservation Program.

title: Protest to Progress: Righting Centuries of Wrongs in Federalsburg
author: Staff Writer
content:
Protest to progress: Righting centuries of wrongs in Federalsburg

 December 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Federalsburg last week took another step toward righting two centuries of ignoring its Black residents.The town unveiled a plaque commemorating the town's progress driven by a lawsuit requiring an overhaul of the election system that systemically prevented the election of Black council members for 200 years.
The court settlement announced in April was heralded as a landmark victory for Black voting rights.
The sign was one part of the settlement, which included an apology from the town.
"The Town of Federalsburg formally acknowledges responsibility and expresses its deep regret for actions and inactions contributing to racial discrimination and exclusion of Black residents, including its use of an election system that prevented any Black person from holding a position on the Town Council over 200 years," read the town's apology. "As officials of the Town, we accept moral accountability for the harms these actions inflicted upon Black residents, their families, and ancestors before them."
The town's apology concluded: "Through this expression of regret to those who endured race-based hardship and injustice, we seek to turn the page on this shameful history, and to begin a process of reconciliation among all of the Town's residents."
That apology is framed and displayed at Town Hall.
In addition, the settlement included:
Commissioning the plaque "From Protest to Progress: Events that Changed the Face of Federalsburg", celebrating Black voters' historic voting rights victory.Installing a photo display at Town Hall, in collaboration with the historical society and the plaintiffs in the lawsuit featuring Black community contributions to Federalsburg.Restoring the name Brooklyn Avenue to the portion of the avenue in the Black district that had been renamed Gerardi Boulevard.Issuing a proclamation naming Sept. 26 of each year as Voting Rights Day in recognition of Black voters' historic win on that day in 2023, the town's bicentennial year.Establishing a Town Unity Committee of elected officials and residents from each district to focus on community engagement in future elections and matters related to the promotion, engagement and enhancement of the town's diverse community.Establishing an annual multicultural celebration.
The lawsuit was filed as Federalsburg celebrated its bicentennial. It challenged Federalsburg's election practices, including its longstanding use of at-large and staggered elections, as violations of the Voting Rights Act.
The suit said Federalsburg maintained a "white stranglehold on municipal power" with its long-standing use "of a racially dilutive at-large, staggered term election system, rather than a racially fair system that would afford Black Federalsburg voters an equal opportunity to elect candidates of their choice."
In 2023, under a judge's supervision to create a plan that did not violate the Voting Rights Act, town leaders changed the election from at-large representation into a two-district system. The plan called for two of the four town council members to represent the predominantly Black part of town.
The election was held in September 2023, resulting in the election of the town's first two Black council members. Darlene Hammond received the highest number of ballots, earning 70 votes and a five-year term on the town council. Brandy James received 52 votes, earning a three-year term on the council.
After the plaque was unveiled last week, Hammond had tears in her eyes.
"It's a lot," she said, taking a pause, "to think that this small little town was able to stand for the rights of all people, not some people."
Hammond, who was a plaintiff in the lawsuit against the town, said the progress that has been made in the town is "heartwarming" and "breathtaking."
"It's a dream come true for me and for others that (came) before me, that we have established that everybody should be represented no matter what the color of your skin is," she said.
Sherone Lewis, a Federalsburg native and first vice president for the Caroline County branch of the NAACP who was a plaintiff in the lawsuit, called it surreal to be celebrating the changes that have been made.
"But I must say, the struggle continues," she said. "We still have a lot of work to do for diversity, equity and inclusion. I know those are buzz words these days. But I do believe that, because I want this for my children, my grandchildren."
Federalsburg has come a long way in the past year. The struggle continues, but the plaque unveiling was an occasion to celebrate progress.
"This day forever marks a turning point in Federalsburg, beginning a new chapter that celebrates Federalsburg's diverse community," the last line of the plaque reads.
Other Eastern Shore communities would be wise to see that their election results are reflective of their communities.
